A MANY-SIDED man is a man who can always appear to be right side up. Somp. people seem, in fact, to prefer to serve by standing and waiting. No man will think any girl old-fashioned if she laughs at all his jokes. THE fortune-hunter is not so much taken with pretty faces as with handsome figures. IN the eyes of the average woman, a crocheted d'oyly is more impressive than a self-made man. Mosx of us dislike to speak ill of other people, but we can't be expected to cease conversation entirely. RODEETSON : "Page is the most illiterate man I ever saw. Why doesn't he study to improve him- self ?" Robinson : "Fancy, he hasn't any time. He reads all the magazines. No woman is ever quite so old as her dearest friend says she is. IT is generally a sweetheart, not a hard head, that a man wants. Ix is an awful shock to find that we have been polite to people who were not worth it. A YOUNG man is never so much surprised as when he learns that other young men think his sister is good-looking. Ha: Don't you thing it wrong for people to marry their intellectual' inferiors ?" She : " Yes —always wrong, and in some cases quite impos- sible."

MY DLLs Nwan, A ,charming theatre toque, flat and wide in shape, was composed of soft folds of pure white tulle, while its sole ornament was a flexible, quivering feather, simulated in diamonds and silver wire, sweeping round from the front to the back of the toque on the left side, a few strands of white marabout at the back of the diamonds doing away with any apparent hardness. Several of the becoming white lace hats, a lace veil falling over the edges slightly all round, have raised brims underneath composed of a network of pearls and diamonds, the brilliancy veiled by the soften- ing lace. A great deal of lace is used on millinery, and also sable-coloured furs, and ermine, and chinchilla. A flat toque of cream or ivory cloth, with mink or sable fur ad lace, is nice with bouquets of violets under the brim,which is usually of dark velvet in draped folds, partially covered by the lace, and this is a very stylish model.

SOME men are born great, some achieve great- ness, and seine couldn't tell to save their necks how, it happened. A MAN of short stature gave as a reason for his stunted growth that he was brought up as a child on condensed milk. "WHAT was the trouble between you aud young Mr. Softy?" "Why, he said his brain was on fire, and I broke a hand grenade over his head." "HURRAH!" cried the millionaire of Yukon City. "See what my friend has brought me !" And the overjoyed Crcesus waved a mutton-chop in the air. It was indeed a blessed gift. ARTIST : "Now, give me your candid opinion of tills picture." Critic : " It is utterly worthless.' Artist : "Yes. I know your opinion is worthless. but I am curious to hear it nevertheless." The newest stocks for wearing with plain silk or cashkes—re blouses in the morning are made of soft satin, with deep stock neckband, inlet with trans- parent squares or diamonds of lace, and two kkjuare ends, similarly inlet with lace, brought from behind, simply crossed in front, and fastened with a jewelled pin. There are some smart ties, too, in black and white tambour lace, with scalloped edges, which are tied stock fashion round the neck, the ends passed through an enamel and paste marquise ring, and then left to hang loose. There are a great many novelties in belts, for the belt is a most important adjunct to the set of a blouse nowadays ; one of the newest is formed of three or more narrow strands of elastic webbing, stud- ded with small steel or jet points, all radiating from a long narrow ornament in the centre of the back, and merging into a one-inch wide ba.nd to- wards the front, where it is fastened by an orna- mental clasp.

AMERICEN MODESTY. —No one equals the thorough-going American in his modest estimate of himselt and the United States in general. A Bostonian was once heard humbly to assert that "he did not suppose that there were 10 men in Boston who were the equals of Shakespeare." This was by way of a graceful concession to the old country. whispered the heroine in the melo- drama, " the villain still pursues us." " Ha," ex- claimed the lover. "But fear not. See thou the ravine that intervenes between NS and him" "Yes, Horatio, but the bridge. He can Cross you bridge at a bound." "Fear not, I say. He has got to stop in the middle of the bridge and do a song and dance. Courage?" "COLONEL Buower," remarked a chappie, "is 1 the finest alter-dinner speaker I know of." 1 "Why ? " said his friend with some astonishment. " I never heard he had any ability in that direction at all." "Well, he has. I've dined with him several times at various places, and after dinner he always says: That's all right, my boy, I'll pay for it. " A(:Eyr : "My dear sir, do you know how much time you lose dipping a pen into the ink Ten dips a minute means six hundred dtps an hour, or six thousand dips in ten hhurs, and each dip con- sumes—" Business Man: "Yes, I know; I have worked it all out." Agent: "And yet I find you still writ ing in the old way." Business Man : "Yes, I am using the fountaie pen you sold me about a month ago—using it in the old way because it won't write any other way." Agent: "Beg pardon, I'm in the wrong office. Good-day." "Miss WILLISTON," he pleeded, "I am going away. I shall travel thousands of miles before return. May I ask you for your photograph before I go?" Jeannette Williston looked at space and sighed gently. "I don't know," she replied, "why you should ask ins for my portrait." "Our friendship," he said. " Surely that is some- thing." " Ves' she answered; ''that is— sow e • thing. But it doesn't seem to ins that you have the right to carry my portrait near your heart— yet." "Jeannette," he cried, "will you be mine?" "Ah, Percy," she said, after it had oeen arranged that they should be married a week front the following Thursday, "how did you dare to ask me? What reason had you for not fearing that I would bid you go away and never show yourself in" my presence again "1 don't know," he humbly replied. "Perhaps it was intuition."

An example - ,ale prevailing use of fur was a white tulle ball-dress, the deep volant en forme of the skirt outlined top and bottom with a narrow band of zibeline, the top band caught up at the sides with a small head and couple of tails, whilst the flounce itself in between was sewn all over with Louis XV. noeuds in the fur. The bodice had the décolletage edged with fur, with a large tulle and lace bow in the centre of the front, mixed with tails of the fur. The mixture of two such contrast- ing things as tulle and fur is still novel enough to be piquant, but it requires careful handling, and the fur must be applied in the lightest and most judicious manner. The use of moleskin is much advocated this season as a great novelty for shat- mg dresses, motor coats, and boleros; to those who have lived in the country, especially in the hunting centres, moleskin is no novelty for coats. It requires some hundreds of the little coats to make an ordinary-sized cape or coat, and the mole- catcher expects an honorarium—so that by the time the skins are dressed and made up a proper fur coat might have been obtained for the same cost.

winter gowns have the advantage over those of summer in that they are independent of any excessive trimming such as is unduly lavished on thin materials. The short sack coat in broad tail or lamb is a very convenient garment, especially when finished with the fiat, round collar that is so largely superseding the high one this winter. It can be slipped on or off in a monient, and is usually lined with silk. The latest shape in sack coats is shaped a little under the arms. This has the effect of drawing the coat in slightly towards the waist at the back, which makes it much more becoming than was possible with the shape that juttad out in a fold. It is predicted that the evening gown of next autumn and winter will be thickly powdered with jewels, or sequins, or steel beads, or embroidered in sucn quaint de- vices as may suggest the intricacies of heraldry. It is probable that same use will be made of family badges in all such embroideries. . The blouse, of course, owes its commanding influence in the world of dress to its upending adaptability to all possible requirements. Its pos- sibilities, indeed, are so varied that in some of the great wholesale drapery houses the flepartment concerned with it is sub-divided into at least four sections, and a stroll through these under the guidance of their clever, alert managers is in itself an education as to the marvellously complex in- terests and conditions involved in meeting women's wants. White shirts are a distinct sub-section from coloured, and muslins are kept apart from cambrics or ginghams. Next in importance are the woollens, into which flannelettes are admitted, and quite prettily printed colourings are shown. In the higher grades of pure wool, these are the shirts which are in such steady demand for cycling, golf and hockey, and their principal development this season has been in making them with pretty collars and cuffs to match. In silks the varieties are endless.

Crockery clattered, plate and cutlery—solid silver, much of which had come down through genera-, tions of Jacksons—rang pleasantly, and, under the energetic labours of Lizzie and Janef, the table was soon loaded with good things from the larder. There were amazing pies of steak and kidney and rabbit; a huge cold boiled ham, a sirloin of cold ! beef; plates of bread and butter, cakes and pastry; and dotted round the board were cups and glasses —cups for the womenfolk, who would probably be partial to tea, and glasses for Jackson and Mark, for the more manly refreshment of home-brewed 7-le. There was, too, a hot fire in the spacious vate, and altogether, as the old farmer said, it .aieemed a pity that a room like that, which was capable of so much cheerfulness, should have been kept for so long for purposes which, for his own part, he would sooner not be reminded of— reading the Bible on_Sundays, and dying When the proper time came round. Jackson was agreeably describing one or two of the most famous 'of the moribund scenes connected with the parlour, and was just on the point of requesting his people to be seated, when the door opened, and Miss Martha JOikson, with a grim smile, made her way in, amazing everybody by sayinc, that she had been upstairs only to change her !Less and make herself fit for the parlour. "I certainly did think of goin' to bed,' she added', somewhat aggressively, a casual observer might have thought; "but I didn't see why, when I've had so much bother with this supper, I shouldn't come in and help to eat it." "Just what I've been thinkin'," said the farmer, with amazing affability. "I knew your Christian spirit would make you see it in that light. Take the chair opposite to use, Martha, and let me give you a bit o this young turkey." "No turkey for me," she answered, firmly, "nor pie, nor beef, nor nothing, till I've seen everybody else looked after. And now, Lizzie, my dear, and Janet, what will you have ? " She smiled sweetly as she; spoke, but there was that in her look which said as plainly as words that sue was still mistreSs of the farm, and would brook ato rival near her throne. But Lizzie was far too happy to quarrel with her seek to usurp her power—did she not know how much worse the rugged old lady's bark was than her bite ?—and she exhibited so much humility that before supper was half through the old lady was _ „

the hands of -a civilian doctor. .is papers came in due course, and his pay as a soldier. The documents he folded .up carefully, gutting with them what was left of his campaigning kit; then he placed the parcel in a great old chest where his own particular treasures were preserved, and not without a sigh pulled down the lid and turned the lock. "I've been thinking, father,. he said to old Benn when he joined him in the living-room, "that I'd like to spend this money in buying something useful for the Bootas. How does that strike you ? You know they were very good to me, and that the war's pretty sure to ruin 'em. I don't think that just because we were set to fight against one another we should bear bad blood." "No more do I," said the farmer, enerrretically. "It's a very nice idea, lad, an' I should like'to see it done. Isn't it farm stock they're mostly. wantin' ?" "They want pretty nearly everything," said Mark. "You see they'll have to make a fresh start. It'll be a sorry business for 'em." "Aye, a lot sorrier than if they were startin' young an' fresh," said the farmer. "A man can't make two real good starts in one lifetime. But suppose we think of it, for a day, an' then see what we can do?" "Very well," said Mark, "that'll suit me." The next day Farmer Benn explained what he had thought it would be well to do. "First of all," he said, "I should like Prince to go to 'em if he's livin' when this trouble's ended. He'll be pretty well what they call salted by that time." "I think he'll pull through it, poor old Prince!" said Mark. "Aye, I don't fancy partin' AVi' him," said the farmer; "but it would be cruel tryin' to get him back here. Couldn't we write to the Major and ask him to do this ? Would he, thinklou ?" "I'm certain he would," said Mark. "He's a square man, and he knows that Prince is my horse still. Anyway, I'll write and tell him what I should like to be done. You see, I'm on a better footing now, being free of soldiering, and it's more a case of between man and man than officer and private. But take my word for it, it'll be all right." "Well, then," continued Benn, who seemed to have a clear idea of what he wished to do, "your pay would buy one or two very useful things for the Bootas. I'd like lu to send them as your the-

'A few months ago an American citizen without title or office/Undo:o in England, and so apprehensive was Threadneedle-street of his power in the financia world, and of the effect which his sudden death might have on the markets, that certain brokers, to protect themselves in their American investments, immediately took the intraordinary measure of applying to Lloyd's for insurance on his life, 'paying premiums at the rate of thirty- pounds on the theutrand for three months. This citizen was J Pierpoint Morgan. who had just organisrd the mast powerful industrial and financial. institution the world has over known. It me ttn.s not whether he was a large owner in the United States Steel Corporation; as its recognised and actual dictator,he con- trolled a yearly income and expenditure nearly as great as that of imperial Germany, paid taxes on a debt greater than that of many of the lesser nations of Burope,and by employing two hundred and fifty thousand men sup- ported a population of over one million souls, almost a nation in itself. Iron and steel making has long been known as the basic industry. England's greatness and Germany's recent progress were due largely to their ability to produce iron and steel cheaply and in large quantities. Mr Morgan, as iron-master, controlling the world's greatest and cheapest sources of iron supply, threatened the trade and profits of England and Gee- many, both of which had already felt the sharp tooth of American competition. It is no wonder, therefore, that he was regarded at the moment as the American peril incarnate. While in England Mr Morgan bought —whether for himself or for American clients it matters not—one of the greatest of English steamship com- panies, the Leyland line,operating thirty-eight vessels between Europe and America. This move, following so closely upon the organisation of the Steel Trust, was' in- terpreted at first as.s blow to England's supremacy on the seas. It was naturaliand inevitable that Europe should anxiously inquire a s to the further intentions of this mar. to whom the purchase of a great steamship line seemed only the incident of a holiday. Comparatively few people possess any very clear conception of what Mr. Morgan is or thes in Wall-street. Be is vaguely com- pared with Mr.BEene, who is a speculator ; with J Gould, who was a wrecker ; with Hill and Harriman. who are strictly railroad men ; with the Astor, who are primarily real-estate owners ; with Carnegie, who was an iron-master. But Mr Morgan's business is purely that of a banker—a worker with money. As such be acts as an agent for rich cleats in the investment of money ; he loans, borrows, transmits money abroad, issues letters of err dit, and buys and sells securities which are the evidences of money. The extensive foreign connectienr of J P Morgan & Co., enable the firm to do a large tueincss in foreign exchange.— " Windsor Magazine. "

herself again and entirely mollified. The old farmer refreshed himself steadily and well, urging his companions to profit by his example, seeking subtle opportunities to snake reference to Mark and Lizzie which no one troubled to try and understand, and generally exercising all his powers to make this feast, the result of his own wonderful' and elaborate planning, pass off well. But it was not needful for him •to trouble, inasmuch as, all suspicion of irritation had vanished even from Miss Martha, who want so far as to admit that young people were young people, and she supposed would go and get married, in spite of all the sad examples they had constantly before them. "Now the point is," said Jackson, pushing back his chair when he perceived that the meal was quite ended, "what's to be done ? I want to go across an' see Mark's father, an' I expect Mark doesn't want to go back just yet. Suppose you an' me go together, Janet; an' thep they can continue their talk. I fancy they've a lotto say to one another yet. As for Martha, I daresay—' "If everybody'll get away for half-at-hour, I'll ,„;:aar this parlour, an' then be off an' say good- night. I shan't be seem' anybody when once I shut that scullery door," said Miss Jackson, determined t 6 maintain the amiable attitude she had adopted, and resolved at all costs not to inter- fere with Mark and Lizzie. So it howened that within half-an-hour Jackson was with harmer Benn, talking over certain things with him—notably as to the best arrangement to be made for Mark's and Lizzie's marriage; Miss Martha was busy in the seclusion of the scullery, keeping a special eye on the silver, and Janet was telling her mother Of the triumphant gathering at Jackson's farm, and incidentally wondering what she should wear at the wedding as a bridesmaid. The two old farmers talked long and earnestly. They were shrewd and experienced men, men who had inherited their farms from their fathers before them, and had improved the values of the proper- ties enormously; they were well pleased to think that the product of their joint sagacity should be for the benefit of Mark and-Lizzie, not forgetful of the claims of,Mrs. Benn, Janet, and Miss Martha. It was settled that, subject to Martha's life interest in the farm, Jackson's place should go to Lizzie unreservedly, on the passing of the present owner. "And that can't be a question of many years," said Jackson, quite unconcernedly, and speaking of himself as he might have spoken of a worn-out horse whose work was done. "God save ale from becoming a burden to my fellows, an' a dotard; may Ile take me off before therm," added Jackson. "'Besides, I've had my enjoyment of the farm, an' don't want to stand in other people's way. Now that that's done with, what about Mark? I don't quite reckon up how he stands. He's still a sowjer, isn't he ?" "I believe so," answered Farmer Benn, un- willingly; he did not like to think that the country had still any claim on his eon's services. "There's some talk of his going away for an operation." "Oh Is he ordered?" asked Jackson. "Yes," said Benn. "I'll confess I don't like it! if he wants a doctor, I can well afford to pay fat one for him." "I don't fancy that he's like an ordinary reg'lar sowjer," said Jackson. "I fancy he's in a special class ; wasn't it for as long as this war lasted, or for twelve months ?" "Some such arrangement," answered Benn. "Well, as he's only a Yeoman, couldn't he be got off—that is, ask to be discharged, an' tell 'em he's no good for any more service, as he certainly isn't, with a leg like that. He can do odd jobs, an' such like, but he'll'be long enough before he's fit for a run or a saddle, to my thinkin'." "It isn't a bad idea," Said Benn, slowly. "They must be so full up at their hospitals that they'll be glad, surely, to be rid o' Mark." "Try it on ; they'll happen let him off, if they think they can save his pay—he doesn't want it, Vrn sure, said Jackson. "I don't think he'd want to handle blood- money," replied Berm, his old rebellious instincts at work again. He loathed war and au its attributes. "I'm still sorry he ever went." "Don't say that, don't say that," protested Jackson. "It's been a sorry business for a lot; an' it's undone some—young Brigg, poor chap;_ but it's made a man of Mark, an' it's done good to Lizzie. I can't explain it, but I've seen a change in 'em both. Liz went off a bit of a flighty lass, but there's no more flightiness in her; Mark went off unfinished, if I can put it that way; but, as I've said, he's come back a made man." "Aye," agreed Benn, "there's that about both their faces Which I can't explain; but you'd know, to see 'ern, that they'd seen a lot beyond what men

you own present. Beyond that I'd like you to get these an' send them on in my name, as soon as ever the war's done an' you can manage it. Of course, there'll be no chance yet." He handed a small paper to Mark. "But," exclaimed the young inan, "you're pretty well sending out enough to start a farm." "That's my idea, lad," said the old man. "It'll cost a lot—a lot to begin with, and a lot for carriage," said Mark, rather dubiously, thinking his father might haye made a mistake. "I know that," said the farmer, quietly. "I've reckoned it all up. But I think we can manage it." "._"l'm not begrudging a it. Heaven forbid " said Mark, earnestly. thought you mightn't quite have understood it as well as me, seeing that I've been there. It's a grand present." "If they're as pleased to get it as I am to give it—or say, as we are—we shall be satisfied, Mark. Now then, what did the doctor say when he came this morning ? " "He thinks the bullet will soon-work down far enough for him to get at it without much bother, and that once it's out, I shall soon be as right as a trivet. I don't mind how soon, for I don't care to feel that I can't look after thrngs as I used to. When they get the bullet and I get my medal, as I believe I shall, I shall just put 'era with the war things to look at sometimes and remind me of what I've gone through. But, do you know, I sometimes feel already as I really hadn't been to South Africa, but had dreamt it all? I'm pretty certain that the feeling will grow what' I'm quite myself again." "Well:" said the farmer, "I shouldn't worry to remember it. There ard lots of things in my life that I try to think about as litqe as I can, and I should do the same with this war. When a plough or rake has done its work it's put away, and this Yeomanry has done' its work." "But there's no need to be sorry altogether," said Mark, cheerfully. "Look, what it's done for Lizzie and for use. It's made us more grown-up in six months than we should have been in sixteen years it we'd just stuck here. It's taught me a lot ,of things—that the Yeomanry ars a vast deal better than people thought 'ern, that dri enemy isn't as bad as he's painted, and that there's no place like home." "Then all I can say is," answered the old man, "that if we've learnt all that, we haven't paid too much for it. ' The days passed swiftly after that—too swiftly for the work which Lizzie and Janet and Mrs. Benn and Miss Martha Jackson had to do, for the wedding day had been fixed and all the arrange- ments for the new life made. Mark and hisiwife had the choice of living either at Jackson's or at Hill Top Farm, and they wisel.y declined to do either, preferring to take over a small cottage on Benn's property as their own most private dwelling until such time they hoped it was loya: distant—as either of the farm- houses became their residence in succession to the living owners. • One day—not till the surgeon had operated and reit:to-cantle bullet—a letter came for Mark from South Africa.. The envelope was addressed in the Major's precise and clear handwriting, and, unopened, Mark carried it across to Jackson's, so that he and Lizzie could read it together. "I hope it's good news, Liz," he said. "But I'm such a duffer about these things. I'm always afraid of a disappointment. So you read it out." "If it's from the Majcr, it must bohll right," said Lizzie. "I'm sure lie wouldn't disappoint you about Prince. As for anything else, I don't see what he can have to say to disturb us. My dear boy, you're beginning to suffer from nerves much too early. Well, here's what he says ; you see, he begins quite nicely " 'Dear Mr. Benn,—l got your note about Prince. He's alive and well ; in fact, he's so hardy, I question whether he'll ever die. lam glad to hear of your return to civil life. I some- ' times wish I was back .again in, the dear old country; but I shall stay here and see this thing through, if God spares me. " 'I will, when the Commander-in-Chief has no further use for the horse, hand him on for the Boer people you mention. It is a curious request, but that, of course, is no business of mine. •" 'I tan sorry to say that several of our brave fellows have gone under, what with fighting and disease. I happened to be at the base hospital recently, and what I saw there made me very sad. " 'By the way, I heard of the death of a doctor there called Donald; overwork, I think, helped on by fever. Perhaps you came across him. " 'Accept my congratulations on your coining marriage, and my best wishes for your happiness.'" _ . For a few moments there was perfect silence. Then Lizzie, in a low voice, said: "There's a saying in the Bible, Mark, that I should like to alter and apply to this terrible business. You know how it goes: 'And there shall be no more sea.' I wish we could make it read: 'And there shall be no more war,' and that we had the nower ra make it so." "Amen," whispered Mark. - [TnE Exo.] •

in a day or two, an' we'll see what comes of it." Jackson went from Hill Top Farm to his own dwelling. It was now eleven o'clock, in his eyes a most unseemly hour to be out of bed, and he was beginning to feel sleepy and tired. All the same, he was resolved to let Lizzie and Mark finish their talk, even if they remained up all night for it; but he was spared the exercise of such forbearance by Mark declaring that he must be going, or he would know about it when he got home. "You see," he said, cheerfully, "l've got more used to discipline now, and mayn't kick against it so much as I might have done a year since." "If we were all as ;well disciplined, we shouldn't rise so far wrong," said Jackson, opening the door 7*.r Mark and assuring himself that he was able to mate his own way home. There were cheerful "good-nights" between them, and Mark, with the help of a thick stick, walked back to the farm at the end of his first day at home after his campaigning.
CHAPTER XXVI.
NO MORE WAR.

For a week or so after his return home, Mark received an amount of attention which embarrassed him. He was essentially a modest man, and disliked publicity of this sort. No.. did he encourage it, for he had a feeling, which grew upon him rapidly, that he had only done his duty as a soldier amongst many, that it was absurd to single him out for notice when %here were so many more whose claims were so much greater. He there- fore said as little as he could in reply to questions, assuring people that they would learn far more from the newspapers than he could tell them; and as those he dealt;with were as brusque as himself be was soon spared further trouble. Mark wished, too, now that, as he believed, he had dome entirely with the war, to forget it and devote hicsaaelf heart Ind soul to farming again. He had proved that he was a soldier, he had kept his word, and he was satidsdi 4ie futurs was as a vaarried man wilis

THUM:LAIC AND BADEN POWEEL.—A passage in Dichect's brief tribute to his brother novelist will be recalled " I vmerriber his once asking me with fan- tastic gravity,Netien he bad been to Eton, where my eldest son thou was, whether I felt as ho did in regard to never seeing a boy without instantly wanting to give him a sovereign. I thought of this when I looked down into his grave, alter he was laid there, for I looked down into it over the shoulder of a boy to whom he had been kird." Another Eeglish lad to whom that " hire ruses of eoui," as Carly ie dasciibed Thackeray; with its beautiful vein of genius," gave a golden guinea still treasures it among his most valued treasures. He is now known as one of the foremost heroes of the South ' African War—General Baden-Powell.—From The" Corn- hill Magazme," for January which contains the second portion of General James Grant Wilenn's reminiscences of '• Thickeray in tha United States." These comprise a number of original letters from the novelist ; and, in addition t) five full-page illustrations and eleven illus- trations in the text, there is a portrait (hitherto unpub- lished) of Thackeray from a sketch by Count D'Orsay. Reverting to old tradition, the Magazine starts the year with two new novels in serial form—" The Intrusions , of Peggy." by Anthony Hope, and "'Use Four Feathers," by A E W Masem—and fiction is further, represented by a short story from the pen of A T Quiller Coucb. There is the usual instalment of the "Londoner's Leg-book " ; Mrs Woods contributes a West Indian study, " At the Justice's Window" ; Mr G S Street has an appreciation of the famous Duchess of Marlborough, and Mr Innes Shand writes on Rigby, the eighteenth- century politician whose name Disraeli fitted on to Croker,

The abolition cf Drawing Rooms, and substitution of Courts is welcomed by all except the RouveaNx riches, and their agents, that is those who in some form or other, have paid to be presented. Henceforth each lady presented will be the invited guest cf Royalty, and the Courts will be held in the evening, as is the case with the Drawing Rooms at Dublin. The public will be deprived of that interesting spectacle, the long line of carriages with their fair occupants shivering in the grey light of a bleak March day, but the change will be a very welcome one to the nervous and trembling debt: tantes. Instead of wating about in the cold, and struggling through the mush of the ante-rooms, they will go straight to the reception apartments at Buckingham Palace, and at night, when those in full dress both look and feel at their best. The idea of evening Courts i 3 not a new one, as it was the custom in the reign of William IV, but the rule that everyone must be first ir.vited through the Lord Chamberlain is altogether new in Court annals. The opening of Parliament in State by the King, and the announcement that the mourning for our late Queen will be suspended for the occasion, will give the Peeresses a freedom in the matter ot dress which they have not had for the past eleven months, and they will certainly present a very brilliant spectacle in the House of Lords. The Court dressmakers are jubilant over the early commencement of State, and other functions, and are expecting a very busy season. The Royal balls and concerts will be upon a scale of splendour unknown to the presont generation, whilst the most brilliant society gatherings will be seen at Ascot, the opera, and other entertainments. Smart and fashionable gowns will he very elaborate for the coming season, and con- sequently this order of things may be expected to descend, and become the vogue amongst all classes of

society. Further consideration hag been found necessary, with regard to the dress to be worn by peeresses at the Coro- nation, and to one who has seen the models shown at Norfolk House will be surprised at the notification that all preparaeons should be suspended peeiding fresh authorised instructione on the sutj et. The two principal points which have to be considered are, that the Corcna- tion will take place at a time of sear when we may expect midsummer weather, and also that the spec. available in the Abbey is strictly limited, and therefor:, not suitable for lengthy trains. Some modifications are now contemplated in the details of the dress, and the Queen recently had a consultation with the Duchess of leucclench on these matters. Lie present D uchese, like the late Duchess of Buccleuch, held the privileged post of Mistress of the Robes at :the Court of Queen Victoria, and no one is better qualified to give an opinion on the subject of the Coronation Robes. Many people believe that there has been a great fall. log off in the number of Christmas and New Year cards and this opinion seems to be well founded, in spite of what the stationers say to the contrary. If anythinn, the Post Office has been more disorganised than ever by the pressure at work, and this is evidence that there is no decline in the practice of sending .seasonable greee- bogs, but a very great number of people now send private cards which answer tbe purpose just as well, For many years, the number ot women postal worker, has been steadily increasing in this country, and the reports of the Postmaster-General have been uniformly favourable to their employment. 'Die, however. has not been found to be the case in Fiance, and the authorities have now decieed to discontinue the em- ployment of women in the French Post Office. Many branches of the department were opened to women workers, in 1893, and the proposed return to the former state of things seems to be based upon the frequent de- mands for leave by members of the feminine staff, and the fact that three women are necessary to replace two men. In Germany, on the other band, women are being much more readily admitted to the Government departments, though hitherto, that country has been the most bin:Aswa!d of any, as regards the advancement of the busine S 9 woman. It is astonishing to learn that as many as thirty to fifty children lose their lives every week, through their clothes catching fire at unguarded fire-places. The u=e of flannelette has greatly iecreased the number of accid- ents. Flannel is slow of etaking fire, and indeed difficult to burn, but flannelette ignites on the sligh,'est contact with fire, and blazes up instantly. It is therefore meat advisable to strictly avoid flannelette in the making of children's clothes, and in fact the danger to life is so ' great that it is surprising the manufacturers do not I alter or reelopt some new process of making it less inflammable. Such lezends as " 9ov-raping Reductions," " Great Bargains,' &c., meet one's gaze in approaching steer.- land, where crowds of eager pushing wennen may be seen; all bent on securing stems below their original price. Icside the shops, hemmed ia between masses of struggling feminity, one sees heaps and heaps of lovely things, the majority with the bloom rubbed eft, but this alas, is+ a mere detail to many aeale-loving woman. The. t there really are some " sweeping reductions," how ever, is perfectly 'correct, but one needs a list and a steady head when sallying forth, and a firm will to purchase nothing but what one really requires. Odd lengths of pretty silks and satins, suitable for blouses, shirts, and petticoats, good artificial flowers for evening garnitures, lanle of all kinds, furs, and lengths of ribbon, all are safe investments. But in the selection of gowns, coats, and headgear, much care is necessary, even when such gar- ments are intended for immediate wear, Nearly every fur coat in evidence at the present time, leaves the front of the neck and the chest unprea . tected. This is a very dangerous mode indeed, and a I quite unnecessary one. The all-important little touch of lace round the throat and down the front can so easily be applied over the closely fitting coat, when the effect is almost, if not quite as good. Many a cough and cold is due solely to these open necks, and we therefore should de well to avoid them. Never was ye lvet more in request than at the present moment and velveteen too is enjoeing a wide vogue. One item to regret is the tendency to plaster these fabrics with many and varied forms of trimmings. Lace and fur are the only items which should be per- mitted to adorn such materials, and the quantity should he strictly limited. Black velvet this winter is almost a livery, as was white satin a season or so back. An eaperlment in ce-operative housekeeping is to he tried in London with a view to providing a number of business women with suitable lodgings. The idea which has been started by a few lady cepitalistsas upon the lines of a private bearding house, a large house be - log taken and furnished and a responsible housekeepsy appointed to look after and manage the home. Each resident would have her own private room, leaving the dining and drawing rooms to be shared in common Erverythir g would, of course, depend upon the manage- ment, but, if well looked after, such homes would cer- tainly offer greater comforts and more social intei - course than private lodgings, while they should come less expensive when the cost is shared by ten or a &nu residents. . ,

OPENINGS IN CA/WM.—The Canadian Government is again drawing attention to the o t ppor _uni presented to settlers in the various Provinces of the Dominion. It is pointed out that in the older Provinces there are Crown Lands and improved farms which can be ob- tained very cheaply and on easy terms of payment, while in Ontario, Manitoba, and the North West Territories, grants of from 160 to 200 acres of excellent land are given free to those who undertake the very light [settlement duties. Agricultural operations in Canad are distinguished by the high average returns they sacure. The present year has again witnessed a bountiful. harvest, and nowhere have the resulta been more satis- factory than in Manitoba,where a total grain crop of over 1 85 million bushels was gathered, from which 45 million ' bushels of wheat alone will be available for export. It is not surprising that these advactages are each t ear attracting increased attention from those who desire to become independent by cultivating their own land The two things which appeal moat strongly to the majority are fear of poverty in their later years and the wish to give their children a start affording fair pros- pects in life ; to such and to those looking for a large - field for their energies or a greater return on their capital, the opportunities awaiting them in Canada should appeal. The illustrated pamphlets now being distributed free by the CANADIAN GOVERNMENT AGENCY, 15, Water-street. Liverpool, give an account of the marvellous develorment which is now taking place in the Dominion, and they will be found interesting and Instructive readina by all. Ha PREFERRED NlCE.—Bere is a stery of a certain Bishop up North who, after a severe illness,was ordered South by his doctor. "Impossible," declared the Bis- hop. "There are dexens of confirmations approaching ; it would not be conscientious on my part to leave here at present." "Itis a case of heaven or Nice, my lord." said the doctor, seriously. The Bishop remained silent for a few moments, then he said, briskly. I, Very w.ll. I prefer Nice." And to Nice, says " Week-End," he went.

A QUEEN'S SOLDIER,
BY WALTER WOOD,
Author of "Barrack and Battlefield," "Fa,mnus British Warships," "Throng} Battle to Pro- motion," "A. Captain in thd Fusiliers," "A. Soldier of the Letion," &c.

CHAPTER XXV, lIOME AGAIN. Sitting there in front of the cheerful blaze, with her head resting on his shoulder and his arm round her waist, Mark listened to Lizzie's story of what had happened since they saw eacls other last in hospital. it was so simple that he might have guessed it from what had passed at Hill Top Farm. Lizzie, in the eyes of the surgeon, had appeared suddenly to collapse under the strain and anxiety of her work, and consequently she had been ordered home. She had left Capetown, on the homeward voyage, as she had left Southampton on the out- ward journey, by one of the mail-boats, later than the sailing of the slow old transport, and she had been home three full days already when Mark got back. It had been really due to' her father that this surprise had been prepared for the trooper. Jackson, it seemed, Was little more than a mono- maniac in hi g declining years in the matter of surprises, and he considered tkat to allow Mark to remain in ignorance until the actual moment of reunion would be a Masterpiece of dramatic construction. Efforts to laugh or reason him out of his fancy had been useless ; he had been proof even against the terrors of his sister's tongue, and his scheme had been allowed to blossom into perfect triumph. In the scullery, which ti'.9 really a second kitchen, large, spotlessly cV, Ind comfortable, Jdckson from time to time reseeeed his pipe front his mouth and croaked "Ho, ho!" at the same lime taking credit to himself for his performance. nhere's nob'dy thought I had it in me!" he declared. "I'm seventy-two years old come next Boxin'-day, an' if you ask use, I tell you 'at I think 'at a plan like that ',lid be no disgrace to the sainclsof a man of twenty-seven." "To my mind," said the sister, whose mittened hands were busy knitting, and who was looking, for her, dreamily into the fire, "there's a lot too much fuSs made nowadays about trifles." "What' sort o' trifles?" demanded Jackson, aggressively. "Do you call this affair a trifle?" "Well, what else is it ?" inquired the sister, facing her brother. "Isn't Lizzie as well now as ever she was, an' isn't Mark, too, bar a bit of a stiff knee?" "A bit of a stiff knee!" exclaimed Jackson. "Woman, do you know 'at he's got a thumpin' big bullet under that knee-cap yet, an' at it's likely to stop there many a long day ?" "Well, didn't owd Doody Booth get a bullet in his body ten year before 'he died, an' didn't he carry it to his grave with him?" asked the sister, triumphantly. "It wasn't a Boer bullet," said' Janet, 'wrath- fully, seeing what she considered to be' a dis- honourable attempt made to lessen her brother's reputation and glory. "No, that's true," said Jackson. ,"I admit it was a bujlet, but, as Janet says, it 'siasn't a -Boer bullet. Are you aware, woman, 'at tie m things explode in a man's body, an' go nigh o smash him up?" He.looked very stern, as he always did when addressing his sister as "woman." "What I say is," continued the sister, undaunted, "that there's too much fuss in this generation. Folk are gettin' too soft. There wouldn't have been a to-do like this in my young days. Don't I remember how our Jack suddenly threw his scythe down in a corner one day an' went an' ? He was away for six year, an' then he came back. They'd sent him home, as he was no more good as a soldier. Did he send telegrams, or make a noise? Not be, he knew better. He just Walked in. I was bakin'. an' so couldn't bother with him, an' he said: Hullo, father, I've come back.' ! Aye,' my father said, so it seems. There's a lot of lost time to make up. Get some tea an' then go an' pick that scythe up an' give 'em a lift in Goodman's field.'" "And did he go ? " asked Janet. "Did he go?" repeated the spinster, grimly., "I should think he did go. I should like to ha' seen him so much as murmur 'at he wouldn't go. Did he go!" The old)ay' wagged her head and communed in silence withsthe fire. z "Well, I wouldn't," snapped Janet. • - "You would if you'd be, n in our house," said the spinster, with terrific iron T. "Maybe," .answered Janet, bridling up. "Oh, no, there's no maybe about it," said Jackson's sister, with exasperating certainty. "Come," interposed the farmer, fearing trouble, "what did for fifty year since doesn't do to-day. Did they plough and thrash, by steam fifty year since? "No, they didn't," said the spinster, "and it would have been a thousand times better now if they didn't use their filthy injuns an' murderin' machines. Fancy settin' steam an' suchlike things loose on the good things that God gave us. Do you think it's right to have injuns thrustin' through the corn an' hay, an' injuns ploughin' up the soil ? The long an' short of it is 'at men are getting' that lazy an' irreligious 'at they'll do anything." The farmer writhed in his chair. "What's this got to do wi' Mark an' Lizzie?" he said. "Who mentioned 'em?" snapped the old lady. "Let 'em alone. They don't want our attentions just now, I'll warrant. Is the supper to be set in , this place or in the kitchen, John Jackson?" "Set it in t' parlour," said the farmer. "We don't want it here at a time like this; an' as for the kitchen, woman, you wouldn't name it if you'd ever had the chance'to get married yourself." Miss Jackson plied her needles furiously. She hovered between the subject of love and supper for the next small battle, and determined in favour of that which was practical, -and not that which was merely an unseen and unknown quantity. , "So long as I'm the missis here," she said, very deliberately, "there'll be no supper in the parlour. There never has been before, why should there be now?" "It's a special occasion," protested Jackson, feebly. "Not in the parlour, John Jackson, not while I'm here." John Jackson rose from his chair. With an unfaltering eye he looked upon his sister and said: "You here or you not here, woman, there shall be supper in the parlour to-night, even if there hasn't been for a hundred years. It's a special occasion, and I'm determined it shall have a special honour. Mark that, woman." Miss Jackson also rose, and also with unwavering glance, exclaimed: "Supper in the parlour if you like, John Jackson, but not laid by me. Good- he collected her needles and walked off to the back staircase. "Dash it!" exclaiine?r the farmer. "Wii-77_ ever such a contrary an' awkward woman in the world"? There!, nobody can say a word to her without her goin' off in a tantrum." "Let her alone; she'll come back," said Janet, in a low voice. "Will she ? 1 know better. She won't," said the farmer, dolefully. "Can I try and fetch her ?" asked Janet. "What do you mean, my lass?" "Let me set the supper. I don't think she'll be able to bear that," answered Janet. "My word !" exclaimed the farmer. Then he smote the table and laughed aloud. "Go it, my • lass; t' young 'tins arg a good match for t' owd 'uns, even yet.' Janet set to work, craftily making as much noise as she could, for two reasons. to warn the lovers and to arouse the spinster. * The lovers heard with unheeding ears. "I'm forced to come through here to get to the parlour," explained Janet, wondering at the hardi- hood of Mark and Lizzie in continuing to occupy the same chair in the presence of an outsider. "It doesn't bother Gs if it doesn't bother you," said Mark, collectedly, although in his soul he rather resented Janet's appearance. "Don't bother, my dear," exclaimed Lizzie, nastily rising, in spite of Mark's attempts to restrain her. "But in the parlour! Why, you must be mad. What does auntie say?" "She says No,' I say Yes," said Jackson, coming in from the back kitchen on seeing that he was no intruder. "There's only one captain of a ship, an' there's only goin' to be one master of this 'ouse." "But why not here ?" asked Lizzie. "Don't you want the parlour usin' ?" asked the farmer. "You used to grumble enough ars.sut it coin' shut up, an' say it was countrified aft' parochial. Of course, if you--" "The parlour, certainly," said Lizzie. "It's just the place, and such a beautiful old room, too." di„Stie bustled about with Janet, setting the table taeparing a wonderful feast. _

div.head: OVERCROWDING PROBLEM IN
div.p: THE OVERCROWDING PROBLEM IN
LANCASHIRE.
Important Facts.

When much is being said of mortality in the concen— tration camps in South Africa, it is claimed by some that it is not greater than in several English towns and cities, notably Birkenhead, Saifora apd Manchester. The overcrowding of populations in working class dis— tricts is a question which will probably enlist the serious attention of local authorities and Parliament in the near future for it is becoming more and more apparent that

if Great Britain is to maintain her supremacy amnia's: the nations of the world her people must be healthy. The housing protlem in the manufacturing towns or. Lancashire presses for solution. The inhabited areas, for instance, of some parts of Stalybridge are so con- gested that they constitute a danger to the residents. It is not surprising to learn that one lady, after living in the centre of Stalybridge for twenty-five years,should ' now find that her health is failing. The lady referred to, Miss Lydiate, was seen the other evening by an Old- ham "Standard " reporter, to whom she gave an account of her breakdown in health, and an explana- tion of the social difficulty under which she, like many another, is suffering. She pleasantly confessed to the reporter that the neighbourhood. of Bolline-street—She
lives at No. 11—is far too thickly populated ; but she said," I am a wcman situated like many another. I have my living to earn, and lam contented to make the best of the conditions.

"I am forty-four years of age," she added, " anC, have always been exceptionally healthy," she explained. " But, about two years ago, I first began to feel very ill. I thought it waa all due to indigestion. I had a pain in .1n! chest, my eyesight became bad, and I always felt worse after I had had something to eat." At this point Mr JQuinn, who was present at tho interview, interposed : "It was weakness and neuralgia." ot I suffered terribly with neuralgia," continued Miss Lydiate ; " and 1 eventualls went into the public 'esti. tution for advice and treatment." _

"Did you improve while in that institution?" in. qu'red the reporter. " Well," she replied, " I must say I felt better at the time, but I was still troubled with weakness. and after I came out I had violent attacks of indigebtion. I fel:: weak and done up."
'But you seem well enough now," suggested thz eporter. _ . _
" Yes, ' Miss Lydiate readily replied, " lam almcst n a well as ever I was, ard i is cwing to taking. Dr. Williams' pink pills. I'll give credit; where credit

is due." " They CP rtaioly set her up," said Mr. Quinn, again taking up the story of the cure. " I was plagued myself, ar d one day I pulled out some of the pills, and rffered them to her. She asked, ' What axe they ?' and I said, ' Dr. Williams' pink pills,' ' Then take them. yourself,' she told me." " But some time afterwards," rejoined Miss Lydiate, " I read in the Ashton '• Reporter " of a similar case to my own, in which a woman had been benefited by taking Dr. Williams' pink pills, so I determined to give them a trial. Mr. Quinn brought me three boxes frcm Astiton,and I took two of the pills after each meal. After I had been taking them regularly for about a fortnight I felt completely cured. The pain in my chest dis- appeared. I now feel Letter than I have done for many a day, and I only take the pills occasionally." " You foll..vr Tour work without suffering any incen- venience ?" questioned the reporter. "I go out working two days a week, and it never seems to trouble me. I have a box of pills unfinished. but it is seldom that I need to take any." " How may pills have you taken altogether ? " "I should think about:three boxes." " You can truthfully say that your present good health is due to Dr Williams' pink pills finally in-

_ . quired the reporter, " and you are not afraid of recom- mending them to other people ?" " Yes I cars," said Miss Lydists, emphatically, " they have cured me, and I can speak well of them, and I have 110 Objection to doing so. They have also done , Mr Quinn a deal of good, and I will recommend them to all I can." Miss Lydiste authorised the reporter to publish, or make what uee of he liked, the particulars she had given him in the interview, concerning the benefit she had , derived from taking Dr Williams' pink pills.

div.head: AFTER THE WAR.
div.p: AFTER THE WAR.

The "Financier and Bullionist," whcso forecasts" have been most accurate of late, is strongly recom- mending South African Land Snares as a profitable investment. It particularly emphasises United African Lands, which, says the writer, " as a Coal-owning as well as a big land-holding Concern ought to stand a good deal higher than its present price of about 45 for the 10s share. The colliery is being worked at present for the benefit of the British Army, but when the War is over it will be in a position to supply the Delagoa Bay Railway and steamers calling at Delagoa Bay with coal. Apart from its coal interests, the Company owns close on 300,000 acres of farmlands, a great proportion of which are said to be highly mineralised." Another promising concern is the South Rhodesian Goldfields, which owns nrarly 1,600 claims In Rhodesia, with the right to peg 1,000 more. All the claims have the advan- tage of being on old workings, and those conversant with Rhodesia know that the old workers always fol- lowed the reefs down until they were drown.3d out, hence it is fair to assume that as they delved so far with- out pumps, the reefs to-Jay must be well worth follow- ing. These shares now oltainable at about 133 63 and United African Lands will, as soon as a settlement is arrived at, rise immediately, and those who take advantage of the present quiet state of the Market must benefit considerably. LOTID ROBERTS'S BOBBY AS A BOY.—When Lord Roberts was a boy, his favourite pastime was carving boats nut of wood. He was quite an adept at this, and he used frequently to wager a vessel of his own manu- facture to beat a beat bought by another lad. All the boats he carved were named after some groat naval hero, or after a big sea fight in which we had been vie- - torious. It is rather curious, adds "The Week- -md." that the man ,who of all others in the latter half of the century has been victorious in the fisld, should have early exhibited a preference for the sea.

div.head: lII3EPLAT, POLITICS 1N 1901
div.p: lII3EPLAT, POLITICS 1N 1901
BY AUGUSTINE BIRRELL, K.C.
As usual, I first turn to the Statute Book, for unless the polities of the past are enshrined in Acts they are not worth talking, still less writing, about. _ c,

One -'great change here awaits us. Queen Victoria's name has disappeared from the back of the volume of the Statutes of, the Realm. Sixty-three volumes, all substantial, though varying in their degrees .of obesity, contain the legislative enactments of the Parliaments of our late Sovereign. The Acts of the Queen are indeed a huge contribution to the body of our laws, and express better than anything else the. enormous complications of ,modern life in its mechanical, industrial, and social aspects. 1 and 2 Victoria grew into 63 and £4 Victoria, and then—farewell Queen. The year 1901 bears on its front another image and superscription—Edward VII. It is a great change, but it has not affected the Statutes themselves; they are no better itrafted than they were before. Were Mr. Balfour a man of business instead of a Inegative philosopher, he would be more con- cerned with the scandal of such a performance as the Workmen's Compensation Act than with the preventior. of obstruction. The fewer such ill-drawn Acts 'of Parliament are passed the better for the credit of the House of Commons. All measures should be referred to a committee of lawyers and grammarians, so as to be made reasonably intelligible,before the King's consent places them in the Statute Book, to be the mockery of judges, the ruin of suitors, and the despair of text-writers. A reform so rational is not likely to receive .11iuch support. If it be asked, Why do not the lawyers in the House of Lords improve the shining hour by making the work of the Lower House at least prima facie intelligible ? the answer must be, Lord Salisbury dominates that Assembly, and shares his nephew's contempt for Acts of Parliament. No oppor- tunity is ever afforded the educated members of the House of Lords to lick a Bill into shape. In the early part of the session,• as Lord Macnaghten put it not long ago at a City diliner, "we have nothinr, to do and plenty of time to do it in: at the end of the session we have a great deal to do and no time to do it in." The retirement of Lord Salisbury is reported to be imminent; it can hardly fail to be beneficial to the business of the country.

div.head: LIBERAL RECORD.
div.p: THE LIBERAL RECORD.
However, King Edward has now completed his first volume. Is there any Liberalism in it It would be odd if there were. It is only -too true to say that in 1901 the Liberal party has achieved NOTHING.

The year found us at war and leaves us at war. It found us spending a million and a- 'half pounds sterling a-week in attempting to bold two countries we have annexed by pro- elamation, and it leaves us spending a like sum in the like attempt. The talk about the war has now got into its third year. From -the King to the crossing-sweeper, from the retired soldiers in the Service Clubs to the poorest returned Yeoman kept out of his pay. nothing else of public interest irr-tallrel,,,bou* but the war. So long as this topic engrosses attention, and whilst this weekly expenditure ran; finance, it would be absurd to expect .legislative activity. What the country wants is to hear that the war is over.

One outside question has, indeed, flickered -uneasily at intervals—the education question. The drowsy Duke who is President of the Council would have us believe that he has been working so hard finding out the differences between primary and secondary education—a task be it observed, as difficult as making head or tail of Sir John Gorst—that he has had no time to follow the history the war; and there are those who believe that he and his "familiar" have actually drafted a measure which is to be considered next session.

This may be so; but, at all events, in 1901 nothing was done. The clergy—that valiant crew—tell us that this time the Government is in earnest, and will use the full strength of a "loyal majority" for the purpose,not merely of introducing, but "seeing through" all its stages a great, though, of course, suspiciously brief, measure which will entrust the cause of national education to committees, with co-opted members of county and borough councils, and will frankly adopt rate-aid to Clerical Schools and sectarian religious education as the final solution of the question. This trifling measure, which Mr. Balfour will doubtless introduce as uncontroversial and a trenchant reform of Parliamentary procedure, will, with an agreeable and popular Budget, a little friendly talk about the war and the War Office, a few Supplemental Estimates, and a suggestion of .Redistribution of Seats, occupy the greater part of the session—but first and foremost will come education. Such is the prognosti- cation of the clergy, who, though super- naturally endowed, are not in a position to _guess what the mood and temper may be of that "loyal majority" which, in January next, will take its seat behind a discredited and unpopular Ministry. The future will unfold itself, and if A 43isregar1s clerical prognostications it will not be for the first time.

THE PARTY POSITION. During 1901 the Liberal party, next to the War, has been the great topic of conversation. In the country, despite heated discussions and a good deal of exasperated feeling, the party has rarely failed to poll almost its full strength. Liberals have been critical and discontented, but have done their duty. The dissatisfied are many, but the deserters have been few. In the House of Commons the ^weakness has been more manifest. A spirit 4::_f_Pedantry and a love for nice points of iillerence have been plainly exhibited. Nobody can tell you wherein Lord Rosebery and Lord Spencer differ about Imperialism, or in what respects Mr. Morley and Mr. Asquith fail to be at one about the obligations of Empire. 'Yet differences incapable of definition, are thought sufficiently Vital to justify the 'establishment of separate and unfriendly organisations hi order to accentuate and perpetuate them. I dareay an immediate prospect of office would annihilate these illusory differences, which at any moment -of friendly chat can be mininiised out of Existence; but in the meantime they make the Parliamentary party ridiculous, and a party that is ridiculous in the House of -Commons is never likely to have any vitry • immediate prospect of oftice About two things the country has seemed to be sure. The first is 'the maddening inefficiency and self-complacency of the King, Ministers ; and the second is the non-existence of a team of competent men belonging to an organised and united Opposition to take their places. Until the whole party works together the country is hardly likely to change its mind on the second of these things, feverishly anxious though it be to express its opinion Ca the first. There must, however, have 'been SonZe Liberal politics in 1001. I think there were suchpolitics ; Bid that they may be described as a long, painful,and wholly unsuccessful effort to restore peace to South Africa. A true Liberal dislikes the state of war, is uneasy during martial law, 'and takes no pleasure in bloodshed. However inuch he may believe in the goodness of his cause and the cleanness of his hands, he seeks peace, and if not fully satisfied that peace is aDossible. he is uncomfortable. Net so the

Tory, who ,is apt t,o think .that war is, a good thing every now and again; that to repeal the Ilecalogue once or twice in a gentury improves the breed; that war welds alt classes together, and clears the air; and he finds in the "realities " of the battlefield an agreeable alternative to the follies of New- market Heath and perpetual polo matches. But history tells us that though Tories go into wars with light hearts, they are ready enough to come out of them after they have had a bellyful of fighting. The most disgraceful peace in English history is that of Utrecht, and Tories made it.

div.head: DESIRE roR PEACE.
div.p: THE DESIRE roR PEACE.

At the present moment there are no Jingoes. The oracles of the music-hall are dumb. Nobody cheers the Colonial Secretary, and the great name of Roberts is received in silence. All want peace, if it can be got. There are only two ways by which it can be got: (a) by negotiations resulting in a settle- ment; (b) by a vigorous and successful pro- secution of the war. These are not mutually destructive methods. Both can be pursued with vigour by men who have made 'up their own minds. Were Lord Kitchener Autocrat, he could, and probably would, pursue both methods at one and the same time. Lord Salisbury pursues neither. HO burkes negotia- tions, allows Mr. Chamberlain to snub Lord Kitchener, and yet is the feeblest War Minister of modern times.

It is said that to permit negotiations would wound the pride of Mr. Chamberlain and Lord Milner. Does the country prefer an income-tax of at least Is. fid. in the L, its food taxed, its trade injured, its social progress impeded, its best blood spilt, to wounding the pride of two men.? This can ' hardly be. , Hitherto all the efforts made by Liberals to secure peace have failed. Disputes as to the origin of the war have largely contributed to the total impotence of the Liberal party during the last two years. It has counted for nothing, though polling nearly half the electorate. The disputes as to the conduct 432 the war in the ranks of the Liberal party are all traceable to differences of opinion as to its origin. Two recent events are at least steps in the direction of peace—the Derby meeting and the Chesterfield speech. If Lord Rosebery really means to be henceforth an active politician, and to take his proper place in the arena of strife, the fact that he does not think with the Derby delegates that it is desirable to recall Lord Milner or to despatch a Special Commissioner need not keep peace-loving men apart; for, as he pointed out with unanswer- able force, the only way to secure the recall of Lord Milner is to cet rid of the Ministry, and that is a feat which is as yet beyond the power even of an united Liberal party. Lord Rosebery's speech breathed a spirit of humanity and sound sense which ha,s been conspicuously absent from the speeches of some of his supporters. Lord Rosebery recognises the difficulties of the situation, and does not repeat the optimistic phrases of Lord Miler's public utterances. He looks into his own heart, which tells him that it will be hard to build a Temple of Peace on smoking hecatombs of slaughtered babes. He agreed to the second resolution passed at Derby relating to tte Concentration Camps, and, though properly firm as a rock as to annexation, he spoke wiser words about amnesty and civil rights and the folly of unconditional sur- render than have as yet fallen from the lips of the politicians who flocked to Chesterfield to get their "marehi'
graeri.".: rovifo -`rel 1-001 should

see no reason why Lord tq)sebery shou, not lead a united party; for as for his Im- perialism, where is the man who would not willingly subscribe to that creed as declared and expounded at Chesterfield? Perhaps before six months are over, an attempt to secure peace may have been successfully made. If peace cannot be made, and the war drags on a couple more years, Mr. Middleton and his wire-pullers will need to beware of their own Jingoes.

div.head: BARREN YEAR.
div.p: A BARREN YEAR.

The first volume of King Edward's laws contains nothing of much note. The fourth Act of the new reign settled the new Civil List. Time was when such a settlement was a risky thing, a mighty delicate and dangerous matter, imperilling even the Protestant succession. We are wiser to-day, and recognise with a deep sense of gratitude the stability and economy of the Throne. The cheap and vulgar Republicanism which flourished at one time in Birmingham and other places has largely disappeared. Presidents have lost their chance. Even Sir Thomas Lipton would hardly do at Windsor. The new Civil List was settled in a few minutes.

div.head: FRESH TAXES.
div.p: FRESH TAXES.

The Finance Act of 1901 is full of policy, if not of politics, and stinks of South Africa. The tax on tea was renewed, and a tax on sugar imposed. This last tax will probably be doubled next year. No man over forty is ever likely again to sweeten untaxed tea with un- taxed sugar. How far off and ironical seems the cry of "A free breakfast table " ! The question no longer is, as in Gladstone's time, "What taxes shall be taken off ?" but, "What taxes shall be put on F" This is un- avoidable if our present rate of expenditure, quite apart from the war, is to be accepted as normal. How are we to raise an annual income of £120,000,000 without new taxes ? What remains to be taxed ? Drink, so the Chancellor says, bears as much as it can stand. Land, so we are assured in a mighty chorus of ruined landlords, needs doles, not taxes. Food only is left. Bread must be invoked to support the burdens of Empire. Let us plant the Imperial Standard on the loaf of the cottager The coal tax was inevitable, despite its inequality and, therefore, unfairness. The Chancellor must have his money. It is idle to complain, unless you suggest either that the money is not really wanted or that it can be better raised elsewhere. If it was not coal, what was it to be ? The income-tax was raised to Is. 2d. in the R—an enormous tax, pressing almost savagely on most deserving people. The pinch of it is already serious; if it is increased it Will become terrible. Yet increased it probably will have to be. Here again the Chancellor's excuse is his necessity. How else is he to get his millions? Tell him, and he will thank you from the bottom of his heart. The sums raised for the service of the country for 1901, as grimly recorded in various Acts of last session, beggar the imagination. Hundreds of millions! It is, indeed, a bumper year! Was there ever such a mistaken estimate of the cost of a war made before! Ten millions was to pay for what two hundred millions will not "see through." DOLES AND SOPS AND DECEPTIONS.

1 Edward VII., chapter 13, is an innocent- looking little chit of an Acts with but three short clauses. Yet it is a thing of some ignificance, for it renews those doles and 60Ps of which we used to hear so much before the toers drove everything except their mobility and our stupidity out of our heads. It will, I hope, be almitted that doles are not Liberal politic but Tory corruption. They are to be kept a ivp until 1906. The sovereigns of the taxpayer and ratepayer still chink in the pockets of the landlords. -

A more romantic Statute r;"ii;.;'c;;;; whereby the King was autlaorised by Commons to assume what titles he chose. It and wisely was a wide discretion; a trusting y has it been exercised. It would have been terrible had the Throne been vulgarised. As it is, the Royal title is now both melodious and signifi- cant. I could wish King Edward no longer dubbed himself Defender of the. Faith, for were he to be rudely asked what particular faith he defended, and where and how and through what Ministers he did it, even hiß

many wit would De at fault to find an effective reply. The Appropriation Act of 1901 contains a grant of £lOO,OOO to Lord Roberts "in recog- nition of his eminent services during the war in South Africa.", The word during is significant. Time was when the war was ova,. So long ago as September 25th, 1900, a General Election being imminent, Lord Roberts was fortunately able to telegraph to the Lord Mayor the welcome tidings that the City'lmperial Battalion and Mounted Infantry would reach London before November sth, and the Battery too, if possible—though, added his lordship, "I fear I cannot return so soon." What was the comment of the Tines in its issue of September 2.7 th ? "Tau WAR IS AT AN END, as is intimated in the telegram of Lord Roberts to the Lord Mayor." On that footing the General Election was allowed to proceed.

div.head: ME EXAMINEE, FRIDAY, JANUARY 3 1902,
div.p: ME EXAMINEE, FRIDAY, JANUARY 3 1902,
SOCIAL LEGISLATION.

The only Statutes that savour of our social state are a Consolidating Factory and Work- shop Act, a necessarily lengthy measure of one hundred and sixty clauses, and an Act to prevent the sale of intoxicating liquors to .children. This tatter Act, probably worthless in itself, illustrates very well the attitude of Tory Governments to the liquor trade. They do Rot mind insulting it, though they will do nothing effec- tually to control it. For • a child under fourteen years of age to enter a public-house to buy Equips, "except in corked and sealed vessels in quantities not less than a pint," is contamination so great as to justify the imposition upon the publican of a fine not exceeding 40s. for the first offence and not exceeding kb for any subsequent offence. What sort of place must a public-house be if a little boy of ten may not run there to fetch a jug of beer for his father's dinner ? And if a boy of ten will be contaminated, why allow girls of fifteen to be exposed to the vulgar jesting and rude handling of the pothouse ?

div.head: EARL GREY'S SCHEME.
div.p: EARL GREY'S SCHEME.

The fact, of course, is the Government is frightened of the trade, and will never tackle it. so it is left to the Bishops and a handful of philanthropists with business instincts to throttle the brewers by competition. It is a fine experiment; am], though it is not likely to decrease the -drinking habits of the com- munity, it may perhaps impoverish the brewers, who now are also the pothouse keepers. I say perhaps, because there is much wisdom in Sir Edward Fry's reminder that if the Bishops' drink-shops su6ceed, the brewers will put their spare capital into the under- taking, and thus make money both ways. The success of the little "public" on the Hill of Beath in my old constituency of West Fife has turned the unaccustomed heads of some total abstainers, who seem to see El Dorado placed at their disposal if only they themselves go into the business of vendors of drink. It would be rash to argue from a place so peculiarly situated as the Hill of Beath that success must crown similar efforts in other places nor have I heard anyone say that the Hill of Beath never sees a 'drunken man stagger along its clectric-lighted path- way. But by all nleans let the experiment be a tried, and such sham legislation as 1 Edward VII., chapter 27 cease to insult our intelligence. AUGUSTINE BIRRELL.

div.head: 7 HE MOST SEVERE WINTER FOR
div.p: 7 HE MOST SEVERE WINTER FOR
YEARS.

--- Reports from the Metecr ological ()Mee predict that the:winter season, on whin we have just entered, will be the most severe we have had in this country for years. An eminent authority on such matters announces that every four years. England is visited with an un- usually severe spell of cold weather, and this is the year on which it is due. Flow to keep warm and avoid colds and chills becomes therefore an irnportan question. The human body mar be said to be heated by a sys- tem of t• toot pipes." These " pipes " are the arteries and veins through which the hot blood is forced by the heart. When ill-health supervenes the blood becomes poor and thin, and does not carry enough oxygen to thoroughly warm the extremities. Cold hands and feet, a et neral sensation of chill, and a shrinking from the least draught are symptoms which reveal this condition. On the other hand the heart may be weakened by some kilmsnt, and rendered unable to pump the blood with sufficient force. Palpitation, fluttering sensations at the Wart, and fits of faintness are signs of this state. There is a tbird common reason for the "warming system" getting out of order. That is the failing appetite. Food is the " fuel " which mends the ire. 1 Whoa the appetite fails the fuel supply is cut off, the beat goes down, clds and chills creep ics and in but too many cases tronchitis, pneumonia, and fatal com- p ications ensue. In Chas. Forde's Bile Beans will be found a strengthening, blood-making, blood-purifying medicine. They strengthen the digestive-organs, thus ensuring that all the " fuel " taken in the form of fool is used. They purify the blood, thus preventing it from carrying about waste and detrimental substances. They cure palpitation, fluttering sensations at the heart, and other signs of weakness of this important organ, thus ensuring vigorous heart action and circulation. Indeecl,in all departments in which wintry weather tries the system, Bite Beaus will be found to give strength. WARRINGTON.
False Alarm of Fire in Scotland-road.

Information reached the Fire Engine Station on Sunday evening that a fire had broken out at the shop of Mr J Banks,outtitter,Scotland-road. Within two minutes of the stopping of the ringing of the bell the hose cart and tire escape had been taken out in the directioa reported. On arrival of the brigade, however, it was found that there was not the least indication of fire anywhere near the premises, and the:reel and ladders were taken back. Meanwhile the horses had arrived, and had been harnessed to the engine, ready to go out. The whole of these proceedings were compressed into a period of about five minutes, and yet some two nundred sightseers had gathered round.the station The gathering soon dispersed , when they were told that it was a false alarm,

- Wesley Guild Social. The members of Bold-street Wesley Guild, held a Christmas social on Monday evening; when about 40 members and friends met in the schoolroom. ,Yarious parlour and round games were indulged in and light refreshments were partaken of .during the evening. All tastes were catered for,and while some of the lighter spirits were marching round to the tune of "Jolly Miller," others were engaged in some of the more quiet parlour games, while others still wve deep in the mysteries of Ping-pong."

Memorial to a Late Warrington Angler. A handsome tablet has been erected m the churchyard. Grappenlmill, in memory of the late Samuel Foulkes, a:well-known War:ington Angler, as a token of respect, by a number of his fellow anglers. After defraying all expenses a very sub- stantial sum has been handed over to his widow, the fund having been carried out by 'a committAe, of which Mr John !I Hackney acted as bon treasurer, and Mr John Wolfenden, as bon secretary Messrs Williams and Clay were entrusted with the preparation of the tablet. Lantern Entertainment at the Workhouse. The lantern entert%inment which was to have de- lighted the inmates of the Workhouse on Christmas Eve, was given by Mr H Taylor, Police Court Mis- sionary, on Saturday evening, and was a great success. The views consisted of photos of promin- ent Warriagtonians. scenery, statuary, Lc, and about 50 mechanical and comic slides which were received with loud applause. A hearty vote of thanks was given to Mr Taylor and to Mr H Thornton who kindly defrayed the expense of the entertain- ment. A wish was expressed that the inmates might soon have another similar entertainment.
