div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOHN CROSFIELD. Biographical Sketch.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. JOHN CROSFIELD. Biographical Sketch.

Warrington is losing many of its most distin- guished townsmen with alarming rapidity. Dur- ing the past few years death has removed many who have been rightly termed Warrington worthies. Names which have been familiar to all the citizens of the town are now but memories. This week we have to record with sincere regret the death of another useful and public-spirited townsman in the person of Mr John Crosfield, J.P., who passed peacefully away at Walton Lea in the early hours of Thurs- day last week. A Warrington man by birth, he realised to the full his responsibilities to his native town, and he has loyally striven to leave it a little better than he found it. He willingly gave his services in all departments of public life. In the Council Chamber, in the Court House, in social and political circles, Mr John Crosfield gays freely of his time for the benefit of his townspeople. For the past two years he had been more or less of an invalid, due to an attack of bronchitis. Whilst returning from his last trip to India hi contracted the malady in an acute form. He decided to stay at Folkestone for a short time in the hope of re- cruiting his health. Here he lay seriously ill for some months but he ultimately rallied and his Warrington friends were delighted' to welcome him back again to his native town, Unfortunately his recovery proved to be but a temporary one, nnd at five o'clock on Th ars- ' day morning be succumbed to a renewed attack of bronchitis, despite the unremitting attention of Dr. Langdale, his medical attendant. He was 69 ' years of age on the 17th of February last. There was the usual family gathering at Walton 14ft on Cl-aistmas Day. Mr Crosfield was unwell, but there was nothing to indicate that the end was so near. During Christmas night he suffered a relapse, and members of the f 2•, qy were suddenly called to his bedside.He was quite conscious up to a few minutes before death, and his wife and his eldest son, 111 r Arthur H.;Crosfield were present when he breathed his last. _ .
" Pure in deeds At last he beat his music out."

Mr Crosfield was the youngest son of the late Mr Joseph Croefield,founder of the firm of Joseph Cros- field and Sons,which was established at Bank Quay, , Warrington, in 1815. He ,was born in the house immediately facing the works. It adjoins the Church of the Sacred Heart in Liverpool-road, and is the residence of the Rev Father Ryan. He came of Quaker ancestors. His mother was a devout woman and her son John inherited some of the characteristics which have been associated with the Society of Friends. He was a man of peace,and had no sympathy with blatant militarism. He re- ceived his early training at York Friends' School, where he remained for five years. Of the strictness of schuols in those days, Dickens and other novelists have given us some glimpses,and those most intim- ately associated with Mr Crosfield have heard from his own lips some amusing incidents connected with his early school life. On leaving York he proceeded to a High School at Glasgow, where he was under the tuition of Dr Dorsey for 18 months. Like ;his brothers he was destined for a business career. His elder brothers George and Morland were already assisting in their father's business, and on leaving school in 1847, John also went to the works. The energy and business-like capacity which was exhibited by the three brothers under the fostering care ot their Lither soon made the name of the firm well-known in the soap trade, and the output of the works increased by leaps and bounds. The progressive career of the firm has been continued until the present day. Mr John Crosfield, stuck to the business to the last, and at the time of his death he was chairman of directors. He was possessed of those business instincts which have helped to build up the trade of this country, and it is some consolation to know that he has left behind him sons who have been trained in the same business school. Not only was he at the head of the firm of Messrs J Crosfield and Sons, but at one time he also occupied the position of chairman of Messrs Brunner Mond and Company, of Northwich, and assisted in the building up of that profitable industrial undertaking. Mr Crosfield earned fok himself the reputation of a kind and considerate employer of labour. To him, his work-people were not so many " hands " ; he knew most of them by name, he freely conversed with them, and those who had grown grey in his service retired on a pension. The first year of Mr Crosfield'a married life was spent at Bowdon. He then removed to Lymm and settled down at Brookfield for a number of sears. In the meantime his brother George had built the stately and elegant mansion at Walton Lea, and on his removal to Lancaster Gate, London, Mr John Crosfield proceeded to Walton Lealwhere he resided until the end. A widow and six children survive him. The children are :—Mr A II Crostield (the Liberal candidate for Warrington at the last election) ; Mr J J Crosfield (who is married and resides at Frods- ham) ; Miss Constance Crosfield (who is at present in India) ; Mrs Major Bales (nee Miss Aileen Crosfield, residing at Jellundur, India); Mr Geo. R Crosfield (a captain in the local Voluutser corps and who has recently returned from active service in South Africa) ; and Miss Gertrude (" Truda ") Crosfield.

div.head: HIS PUBLIC CAREER,
div.p: HIS PUBLIC CAREER,

Mr. Crosfield's public career may be said to have commenced when he entered the Warrington Town Council in November, 1866. Ile was returned as the representative of the South West Ward, now known as St. Austin's Ward. Within recent years, Sankey Bridges has been added to this Ward and has altered the political complexion to some extent. At the time of Mr Crosfield's election it was a Tory stronghold and he was one of the very few Liberals who could win the seat. It was on the sth of November 1866 that Mr Crosfield signed the declaration on acceptance ot office. On looking at the official document we find the affirmation was in the following quaint phraseology I, John Crosfield having b-en one of the p?ople called Quakers having conscientious scruples against subscribing the declaration contained in an Act passed in the ninth year of the reign of King George IV. intituled an act for repealing so much of several acts as imposed the necessity of receiving the Sacrament of the Lord :s Supper as a qualifica- tion for certain offices and employment,do solemnly sincerely and truly affirm that I will never exercise

any power, authority or influence which I ncay possess by virtue of the office of Councillor to injure or weaken the Protest tnt Church as it is by law established in England, or to disturb the said Church or the Bishops and Clergy of the said church in the possession of any rights and privileges to which such church or the said Bishops and Clergy are or may be by law entitled." . _ _ _

No such affirmation is now asked of a Councillor on accepting office, the Oaths Act having rescinded it. Mr Crosfield proved a usetul member of the Council, his business qualities being of great value to the Cor- poration. In 1882, the members conferred upon him the highest honour it was in their power to bestow by electing him Mayor of the Borough. He discharged his Civic duties with the utmost satisfaction and he made his term of office memorable by several handsome gifts, one of them being the School of Art. At the close of the Mayoral year he was thanked for his services and for his unvarying courtesy and imparti- ality when presiding over the deliberations of the Council. Three years later—in 1685, Mr. Crosfield was elected an Alderman otothe Council after a close contest-. Councillor Sutton was brought forward by the Conser- vatives in opposition to Mr Crosfield, and on a vote being taken it was found that 15 members had voted for Mr Crosfield and 13 for Mr Sutton. Mr Crosfield was therefore appointed Alderman in succession to the late Alderman Tbewlis. He continued an Alderman of the Borough until the 28th of October. 1890, when he resigned. Mr Councillor Platt was elected to Eli the vacancy. On the sth of May in the following year, the Council decided to recognise the services to the Borough of Mr Cresfield and Mr Joseph Davies by presenting them with the Freedom of the Borough. The ceremony was per- formed in July of the same year. In accepting the casket containing the scroll, Mr Crosfield said " I shall value it as long as I live and I am sure that those who come after me will value this casket as an evidence of the Council's kindness and friendship." Reference was made in the course of the proceedings to a tour which the two new Freemen had taken together, and in alluding to it, Mr Cros- field said " We have been friends for a great many years, and I am proud to say that although Mr Davies has called himself a stupid old Tory and that I am " a mad Radical," we have never load a cross word between us all our lives. We have travelled over the sea ; we have lived together on steamer for 75 days and no two men ever went a journey and enjoyed it more than we did." In 1E96, Mr Crosfield impelled by the'convic- don that his services would be of value to the Corpora- tion in dealing with the proposed culvert scheme of the Manchester Corporation,decided to re-eater the Council. Be was returned as the representative of St Austin's Ward and was re-elected in 1697. He finally severed his connection with the Corporation in 1900 and he was succeeded by Councillor William Roberta. It will be seen that Mr Crosfield's connection with the Council

xtended over a perio I of 35 years. 1 Mr Crosfield's political principles brought him into greater prominence than even his connection with the Corporation. lEte was an sr leat Liberal and he was in the vanguard of almost every fight since he entered public lire. He was aFsociated with John Bright and Cobden in toe great days of the Reform movement. In the election of 1868 he used his influence for the return of the late Mr Peter Rylands, who wrested the seat from the late Sir Gilbert Greenatl, Bart., who had sat con- tinuously,as a Conservative, for Warrington since 1547. At the succeeding election, in 1874, Sir Gilbert Greenall regained the seat by a maj )rity of ISO votes. In ISSO the late Mr McMinnies again won Warrington for Liberalism. In 1855 Mr William Crostiel lof Liverpool. was the Liberal candidate. hut he failed to hold the seat, and in 1886 Mr John Crasfiell tried, but he also failed, being defeated by the late Sir Gilbert Greens:!. Mr Croseeld's speeches were characteristic of the in in. Blunt, straightforward, transparently honest in his co avietions, he dealt sledge-hammer blows at is oppo- nents. there was nojiac,?e about his speeches ; they were couched in hdrnely and vigorous language and sometimes his express:ons were a trifle strong. Ile be- came very popular as a platform speaker and there was rarely a Liberal meeting held in Warrington without his voice beinp heard. HP was a staunch supporter of the: Liberal cause in Warrington and a generous contributrir to its funds. At the time of his death he was prasident of the Liberal Association, and also treasurer of the Liberal Club.

In educational matters Mr Crosfleld took a deep interest aed he gave liberally of his means for educa- tional inetitutions. The School of AO owes its exist- ence to his generosity. He was one of the managers of People's College School and not only contributed to ite funds but built at his own expense the handsome infant ;school at Bank Quay which is also used as a Sunday school in connection with Bank Quay Working- men's Mission. To this mission Mr Crosfield was always a generous friend. The scholars were always accommodated at Walton Lea on Walking Day and on:other occasions he showed Ifs interest in the Mis- sion in a practical way. Of his other benefactions to Warrington, mention must be made of his gift of the town clock,and also of his thoughtfulness and genero-ity to the townspeople of Warrington in throwing open to them his gardens and conservatories at Walton Lea, in order that they might view his collection of chrysan- themums, az 'leas, and camelias. This privilege was greatly appreciated, and thousands in Warrington have become by this means as 'familiar with the grounds at Walton Les as the owner himself. e- As a magistrate, Mr. Crosneld tempered justice with mercy. Recently ho had not been a regular attendant on the Bench owing to failing health. Ha was appoin- ted a justice of the peace for the borough in 1E74, and ten years later he was appointed a county magistrate. Although honours came thickly upon him, he never sought after them. He carried out his work in a quiet, unostentatious way and cared little for popularity. Although a Quaker by birth, Mr Crosfield became a member of the Church of Eogland. He liked the form I of:service and the nooeic. When staying at Walton Lea, I he worshipped at St Thomas' Church, Stockton II nitts. He held broad religious views and disliked anything in toe nature of sectarianism or bigotry. Personally,Mr Crosfield was a genial and kind-hearted man. Those who knew him best loved him most. He was a typical John Bull and by his death the com- munity has lost a valued servant. Wide and varied is the circle from which will flow.towards his widow and family a stream of heart-felt sympathy in their mast 'sorrowful bereavement.

The grave closed over the remains of the late Mr John Crosfield, J.P., of Walton Lea, on Monday, when the remains were interred in St. Thomas's Churchyard, Stockton Heath. The family grave lies on the south-west side of the churchyard and here the remains of his former wife were laid to rest 21 years ago. In the immediate vicinity are the graves of other relatives of the deceased gentleman. The time fixed for the interment was 11.30 a.m., but two hours previously people began to congre- gate in the vicinity of the church and Walton Lea. 11 he works at Bank Quay were closed and the em- ployes proceeded to Walton Lea to pay the last 'tribute of respect to a kind and considerate em- ployer. 1 The Mayor (14r3 Charlton Parr) had issued an incitation to the members of the Town Council and the magistrates of the Borough to accompany him Ilat the funeral. A large number responded to the invitation and met at the Town Hall, where carri- ages were in waiting. On the arrival of the cortege at toe church gates. the coffin was borne on the shoulders of eight of the oldest workmen of Jlessrs Crosfield's to the church. It was preceded by the choir and the Vicar (Rev II V Pigot). Toe interior at the church was effectively decorated with holly and ivy. The service commenced by the singing of Cardinal Newman's well-known hymn "Lead hindly Light." The opening sentences of the burial service were then read. Psalm xc was chanted and the 15th chapter of Paul's first epistle to the Corinthians , was read. The congregation then joined in sinzing ' the hymn " Peace, perfect peace" and at the close of this portion of the service the organist Mr Rose) played the Dead March in " Saul." ' The remaining portion of the service was com- pleted at the graveside and another hymn com- mencing" On the Resurrection Morning" was sung. The coffin was of fumed oak with handsome brass 'mountings and contained an inner shell. On an ' engraved plate was the inscription: "John Gros- field, died December 26, 1901. Aged 69 years." AN interesting story was related to a Newcastle reporter by James Connell, a respectable bricklayer's labourer, who resides at 84, Blandford-street. Connell, who is twenty-one years of age, is employed at the factory of Messrs. Hawthorn, Leslie and Co. "Four or five months ago," said he, "I began to have curious pains in ray head. Up to that time, I may say, I had had pretty good health. But soon after the pains in the head there came severe pains in the legs and the body, and my strength began to leave me. My appetite fell off; I was dizzy and sick ;my rest was broken at nights. Then, unfortunately, I took a I chill, and pleurisy set in. Of course I had to give up my work altogether. div.head: BATLEY WOMAN'S GOOD FORTUNE.
div.p: BATLEY WOMAN'S GOOD FORTUNE.

A representative of the " Batley News" the other , day investigated an interesting matter concerning Mn Emily Shaw, the wife of an industrious coal miner,wha i lives n Sykes-lane, Soothill, Batley. "For two years I had been ailing with neuralgia," said Mrs. Shaw. "1 kept going to the:druggists for medicine, but was always told that the neuralgia was brought on by weakness, and that I should not be better until I became stronger. The pain was very bad, and I used to sit up in bed at all hours of the night, suffering from it. I had a tooth extracted, but that did not give me any relief. "It was about Cbristmas,l9oo," she went on, "when someone recommended me to try Dr. Williams'lPink Pills for Pale People, and as a last resort I sent direct to London for a box. I gained almost instant relief, and by the time I had taken the contents of three boxes I felt completely cured." "But did the pain recur when you gave up taking -the pills ? " queried the reporter. "I was not troubled with it for a long time," said Mrs. Shaw, "but feeling it come on again I took the pills once more, and this time the pain disappeared very quickly. I am glad to say that I have not suffered since, and I have recommended the pills to others who have suffered as I did. lam now as well and strong as ever I was, and am quite able to do my work."

div.head: SUNDERLAND WOMAN'S ACTION.
div.p: SUNDERLAND WOMAN'S ACTION.

Soma features about the experiences of a Southwick, Sunderland, woman have given widespread interest. Mr 4. Lamb, who lives ac No. 8, Wellington-street, stgrTed to give a Sunderland Herald and Post reporter her story for

" For five years past," she said, "1 have suffered from indigestion. I used to have a severe pain at the top of my stomach and across my back, and I vomited nearly all the food I took. A tired feeling was always with me, and I could hardly get about my housework; I got very weak and nervous. I was in the infirmary for a fortnight, and they seemed to do me some good, but as soon as I got out again I went back to my former condition. But lam a great deal better now, and I can do my housework without causing me trouble, and I can take my food well, and enjoy it." "How do you account for your recovery ?' "Well, I real in the newspapers of cures effected by Williams Pink Pills for Pale People, and as a case was very like my own. I tried the pills. When I ha& taken half-a-dozen boxes I felt a new woman, and all pain had left me. Five weeks ago, after I had taken. some of the pills, a great clot of congealed blood came from my stomach, and since then I have felt well. I should advise anyone suffering from indigestion to take them. 1 recommend them to all my friends."

div.head: LEEDS ELECTRICIAN'S DANGER.
div.p: LEEDS ELECTRICIAN'S DANGER.

An employee at the Electric Lighting Station has had a curious experience. Mr. James F. Cressey, the man in question, resides at 3, Hampton-terrace, Rich- mond-hill, Leeds, where he was seen by a "Leeds Saturday Journal reporter. "Eighteen months ago," said Mr. Cressey, "I was employed at the Corporation Electric Lighting Station in Whitehall-road. One night I was attending to one of the dynamos, when suddenly I fell to the ground. I was unconscious two months. I had no hope, after I recovered consciousness, that I would ever be able to use my limbs again. I had the will, but my limbs re- fused their duty, and I lay helpless and hopeless for seven weary weeks. I had the best medical advice that could be got for money, but every effort seemed to be fruitless. Then a friend told me that his wife, Mrs. Cooper, of 5, Garden-place, Hunslet, had suffered from numbness of the limbs and was•cured by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills.

"I tried them. Up to this date I have taken seven boxes. The first box of the pills seemed to have no effect at all, but before I had finished the third I was able to get out of and in to bed without assistance. At the end of the sixth,l could dress myself without help ; the remainder of the seventh box of pills is there on the sideboard. I don't think I shall want any more,for lam as well as ever I was."

It is strange, and no less A Happy New comforting, with what Year.

- courage and firmness human nature places its foot upon the first step of the ladder that leads to the new and the un- known. No matter how long and dismal may be the record of past failures; the year that has gone may have been shrouded in mists and clouds of doubt and uncertainty, the path of progress may have been barred by adverse circumstances, good resolutions may have been made only to be broken, or may have failed to bear the strain of the critical moment; but the first day of a new year almost invariably brings with it the hope of the dawn of better things, attended by new reso- lutions and fresh determination to do and to dare all that a man may. Thus the 4voll-worn words of the poet receive fresh significance, over re- newed:
" Mips spring eternal in the human breast ; Man never is, but always to be, blessed."

In a pessimistic view it is all very shallow and miserable, this make-believe of good times to come, which seem never to arrive. Seem, we say, for the trouble is that when the good time does arrive, as it frequently does, we take it so very much as a matter of course that we forget the promise of which it is the fulfilment, and even the manly, noble effort or patient waiting that called it forth, and so we miss much that would help us in our philosophy, and serve to turn our earthborn pessimism into the optimism that should shine clear as the sun in the firmament, where it has its origin. The truth is that with- out the ardent longings which go to make up so much of human experience, without the hopes and fears, aye, and even the disappointments,there would be no progress for the human soul. The daily round would indeed become the tread of the horse in the gin, without progress, outlook, or development. Othere than generals have had to admit that they have learnt more from their fail- ures than from their successes ; and in the careful review of past errors lies the best security for future success. Frequently,indeed, even what has been regarded as failure may be but the seedtime of success, the laying of the foundations of which will ultimately prove a substantial and elegant structure of human endeavour and achievement. It is quite true that the contrivances by which we mark offloeriods.of time are mere arbitrary fig- ments, but they serve a useful purpose. They arrest, even if it be momentarily, the course of the thoughtless, who live only to throw away the golden opportunities of life ; they give the wise an opportunity to look back and mark the course of their progress,to study defects and their results they give the unfortunate fresh opportunities to entertain hope, and collect,it may oe,scattered and neglected energies for one more fall with the powers of destiny. They give cause and occasion for reviving hope,invigorating faith, and generally stimulating the human spirit in the apparently; endless struggle against chaos, which really proves the means of bringing out order, harmony, and the universe of the:beautiful from the undeveloped mass amongst which we are at present struggling- , , Thus the new year has a mission of hopefulness; and it is in this spirit that we should desire to greet our readers with a new year motto : Trust God and go forward, In this spirit we wish them Happy New Year."

OF the new Acts of Par- rhe Factory and liament that have come Workshop Act. into force with the New Year, by far the most important is the Factory and Workshop Act. Besides consolidating the existing statutes, thus presenting a complete code up to date in one volume of 163 sections, the new

Act embodies numerous improvements on the pre- viously existing law, which are found in provisions more or less intricate on all kinds of subjects. ID is manifestly in the interest of all those who wilt be affected by the new legislation to make the acquaintance of its requirements as early as pos- sible, with a view to seeing that the advantages it provides are brought into effect by those res- ponsible for so doing. Health and safety are two important essentials to workers, and the pro- visions for securing them have been pushed further than in any previous Act. It is now recognised that besides guaranteeing a certain air space to each worker in a factory it is quite as necessary that the space so provided shall be kept properly ventilated. This is obvioks when one keeps in mind the enormous quanti- ties of carbonic acid constantly being manu- factured by human lungs and poured out into the living or working space, and which science is never tired of telling us requires to be got rid of as quickly at possible if the human organism is to retain a normal state of health. The Home Sec- retary is therefore empowered to prescribe certain standards of ventilation, and to see that these are kept up under the supervision of the factory inspectors. Where workshops are used as sleep- ing-places,then a higher standard of air space must be provided, in consideration of the double pur- pose served. The Home Secretary is also required to ascertain through the inspectors the nature of the sanitation provided, and to determine a proper standard for the same. This will be a most wholesome and much-needed provision. He will see that where wet processes are carried on the floors are properly and regularly drained; that proper means of escape from fire are provided ; that boilers are not only fitted with safety-valves and steam and water-gauges, but that these are imriodically tested and fOund in good working order; and that children are not employed in cleaning any place under moviag machinery, except overhead mill gearing which has been properly secured. Some useful provisions are including regulating the hours and meal-hours of children, young persons, anA women, who are reckoned at fourteen years and eighteen years and upwards respectively. No children will be em- ployed at the age of twelve in future, but those thirteen years of age who have a school certificate may still be employed. The safety of outworkeis is provided for, for the first time. A list of such must be kept by every firm employing outworkers, and a copy must be sent twice a year to the local authority, which may be the town, county, or district council, who have powers confsrred upon them to see that the work is carried on under sanitary conditions, and free from infectious disease. Dangerous industries are dealt with so as to make more economical and efficient the en- forcing of special regulations. Where the em- ployers demand arbitration trades will be classified, and the results of a test case applied to the whole of the trades in a class. This will make it possible for the Home Office to face the opposition of in- terested parties, which has not been the case previously. There are other special provisions with regard to the fish, fruit, confectionery, an d bakery trades ; and altogether it looks as if Mr RITCIIIE had succeeded in getting a great deal of useful legislation into the Act, which it is to be hoped will now have its provisions brought into full exercise by the alert attention of the trades concerned.

In the attacks which are being made upon the trade-union system, some of the more vigorous assailants seem to forget the tremendous compli- ment they are paying to the leaders of the men. According to the writer of the much-talked-of " Times " articles on the " Crisis in British Indus- try," the trade-union chiefs exercise an influence which the master never possessed over his slave in the palmiest days of serfdom. Not only is he able to inflict what Marcus Aurelius would have us believe to be the greatest of injuries in forcing him, by various methods of shirking, to be unjust, but at his bidding the workman is prepared to give up all worldly ambition,to starve,andi see his children starve—in fact, there would seem no limit to the trade-union leader's power. All this argues stupendous ability in the leader; and, if all that is said is true, the real interest ; of the employer might well be to place in a position of higher and yet higher authority a servant of su eh wonderful gifts. We are remin- ded of a story which comes from across the Atlan- tic, and concerns a machine-shop into which some- how or other came a terrible agitator from Trade- Union-town. Letters were received from another district, warning the superintendent of the enor- mous power this man wielded over his fellows, whom he could make do just as he pleased. The superintendent called the man forthwith into his office, and showed him these communications ; but when the poor fellow was expecting miserably his " walking ticket" he found himself, to his amaze- ment, appointed foreman. "Ii you can handle men as these letters say you can, take charge of the shop," said the superintendent, "and see that a full day's work is done." This was a bold way of making use of a man of exceptional ability ; and, unless the teller of the story errs, the result was in every way satisfactory.

--- The woman who is playing the part of hermit on the sea-shore of Argyll seems to be gaining health by the experiment. She takes her morning dip in the sea whatever the state of the weather, and subsists on the most frugal food—indeed, the mystery is that the food she takes proves sufficient to support her. Her success, however, demon- strates the value of fresh air when it can be ob- tained in sufficient quantity, and by contrast it shows the waste and wear and tear of life under modern conditions. Only this week there comes a report from another quarter as to another example of the healthiness of a simple life. An apostle of the doctrine of plain living, a strong, fair-haired German, has appeared in the streets of Rome. It has been his practice for some years to live on fruit and vegetables, to sleep in the open air, and to spend most of his time in walking. He covera long distances without any.fatigue ; and the fine vigorous condition of his muscle and flesh the clearness of his skin, and the strength of his eyesight, all confirm the belief that the man will enjoy a freedom from disease which the wealthy luxury-seekers may envy. Cancer, fevers, and a host of diseases which are probably indirectly due to dyspePsia. haye no terrors for him—so, at least, his contention is. The mistake of most people in endeavourlng to adopt simple habits and diet is that they ir ake a sudden change for which the system is not fit. These things, if they are to be done, must be done gradually. But, after all, the scheme suggests one drawback—a prolonged old age of gradually declining strength.

-- Liberals, Conservatives, and non-politicians alike in Warrington were profoundly sorrowed by the death of Mr. John Crosfield, which took place at Walton Lea on ,Thursday last week after an illness lasting many months. It is only a brief year or two since Mr Crosfield was one of the leading figures in local political and public life, and though of late he has not been seen amongst us, we shall miss him much now that he has de- parted for "the undiscovered country, from whose bourn no traveller returns." Men like the deceased gentleman—of such staunch spirit, firm belief,and indomitable pluck—are rare, and they can ill be spared from this work-a-day world. They are like living sign-posts along the track of ordinary existence, in that they show the way for others to follow. Mr John Crosfield was always a
1- I, e
to 'is I 0 Lit
n- n- e- e-
leader,—and a fighting leader. He led the Liberals of the. town through many a campaign and was ever in the forefront of the battle. There

- _ was something inspiring about his breezy person- ality, optimism, and energy, and he rarely failed to carry an audience with him when in his best mood as a platform speaker—and his best mood generally meant that some party or policy was getting particularly hard knocks delivered straight from the shoulder. Mr Crosfield was a" Liberal without adjectives" if ever there was one, and we never knew a more staunch or unswerving sup- porter of the party of peace and progress. Liberalism in Warrington—though at present a dormant force—owes much to the late Mr Crosfield and it is just possible, had he not been incapacit- ated by physical disability,that it would never have sunk to the low level it stands at to-day. In the last election one of Mr. Arthur Crosfield's chief regrets was his father's inability to render him any active assistance, and this regret was doubt- less shared to the full by the late Mr. Crosfield himself. The measure of his loss to. Liberalism cannot easily be estimated, but there is hope that the son may worthily fill the place of the father. In manufacture too, -Mr. Crosfield achieved great success after very small beginnings, and the huge works at Bank Quay is an eloquent, though silent testimony of his industry and commercial acumen. Though his death was not unexpected by mem- bers of his family, only a few people in Warring- ton had any idea that Mr. Crosfield had been nearing the borderland between this life and the next for some time, and the sad news came to many in the nature of a shock. Warrington, and Warrington Liberals particularly, will keenly feel his loss. At the same time they can and do sympathise deeply with the family thus sadly bereaved.

Volunteers all over the country are much inter- ested in, and many not a little concerned by, the special army order issued by Lord Roberts last week. Opinions vary as to the result of tho new regulations, but the majority tend towards the belief that they will effect a reduction in the numerical strength of the force. Apparently the War Office prefers a smaller number of thoroughly efficient volunteers to the present large force con- taining such a high percentage of partially- trained men. Camp training for six days in each year will be imperative in future, and recruits who cannot spare the necessary time for the requisite training will not be accepted. This will probably tend to check recruiting, and moreover it is possible that many existing volunteers will find it necessary to resign owing to the stringency of the orders. Some battalions will of course be harder hit than others. Locally we should not imagine that there will be much difficulty in complying with the regulations. In this part of the country the volunteer battalions possess a high per- centage of efficients and men who annu- ally go into camp, and the Warrington battalion is particularly fortunate in being able to muster so strongly for the annual training. enerally speaking the new order is in the light of a compliment to the volunteers as it recognises their military value and importance to a greater extent than formerly, but all the results cannot be foreseen. Some authorities profess to see in the change an interference with the voluntary principle and tear even that the iron hand of conscription is reaching out towards the volunteers. This is probably ridiculous, but it is too hazardous to attempt to guess just now at what may be the outcome. of the regulations. The intention is good and it is to be hoped that the result may be bene- ficial.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

Of the two faces of Janus most of us prefer that which looks forward to the future, and now that we are fairly launched upon the broad waters of 1902, which the pen is becoming accustomed to trace at the top corner of our letters, it is well to believe that the Present Year will be better and brighter for us than any that have passed. Al- though there may lurk a trace of unbelief in the minds of some of us, born of experience and jar- ring upon more cheerful ideas, just as the discord- ant whistles of science and commerce bring one's thoughts to the level of mundane affairsovith their uncompromising realism, yet experience teaches disillusion. Bright bops, it is true, are not always realised. The first week of a new year is very much like the last week of the old year, and " the future is but the past, entered by a new door." But experience teaches also that fears, like hopes, are exaggerated, and that the course of events gener- ally reveals that if our day dreams are unrealised, so also are the most serious anticipations. Perhaps at a time when there is so much to alarm, or at least to discon- cert us in our general and national condition, it is the lesson of reassurance that can be most wisely and properly learned at this period of change from the old year to the new. No saying of compara- tively recent origin has become more trite than Lord Beaconsfield's dictum, " it is always the un- expected that happens." Far ever since common experience was crystallised in this phrase its truth has been continually illustrated. Illustrations in- need are too numerous, in the language of Cheap John, to mention, and the very latest may be ob- served in the appearance of that distinguished Japanese statesman the Marquis Ito, as guest of London's Lord Mayor, at the Mansion House on Tuesday. A very few years since,?comparatively, no one could have anticipated a visit of this kind from the Far East, anl it requires no great effort to find similarly unexpected and propitious happen- !rigs within our own domestic circles; and 83, there 58 reason to believe, it over will be.

-- In the question of Artny Recruiting the provinces are greatly and directly interested,and,from a fore- cast which has just appeared, many will be con- cerned if not surprised to find that the figures show s, considerable falling off in the number of men who have joined the colours. Notwithstanding the Somewhat modified requirements of the War Office, the percentage of rejections, chiefly on medi- cal grounds, has been high. Pessimists may feel encouraged to make play with the bogey of physical decadence at this report, more especially when they find that the number oi men " specially enlisted "—i.e. under the standard weight—has been greater this official year than ;last. This, of course, does not compensate for the fewer enlist- ments of what may be described as "statutory loen." One of the explanations for the falling off in the number of recruits naturally is that many of the better class young men who might have en- rolled themselves in the army under ordinary regu- lations have been attracted to the Yeomanry by the better pay and leßs irksome conditions of service. Thus the War °lnce may read a useful lesson,since the flocking of first-class recruits to the Yeomanry suggests that there is room for improvement in the conditions by which the day's work in the perman- ent regiments, horse, foot, and artillery, are regu- lated. It seems absolutely essential that any , scheme or any reform, to be thoroughly successful must be commenced more ;with the individual, and less with those generalisations under which the pritish army is assumed to be a vast" ~,le machine" everybody was , To military enthusiasts the document l prove Particularly disappointing, and only a supposed to be a very short time since. " military enthusiast

--- North countrymen will be pleased to observe in the list of names of persons-composing the latest Royal Commission on the:Coal Supply,tbat oflDir W I L Jackson, M P, managing director of the Great Northern Railway with whom is associated Sir George Armitage, chairman of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway; and there are other names which the reader may have seen previously men- tioned in discussions bearing upon this important -question, au that of Mr C Le Neve Forster, one of his Majesty's inspectors of mines. The primary object of this new Commission is to inquire, not so much into the question of how Great Britain is to continue furnishing he world at large with a cheap supply of the "black diamond," as to ascer- tain how long it will be before this country is reduced to importing the coal it requires for indus- trial and domestic purposes. A little fuss appears to be made about the publication in the daily papers of the names of the Commission before it bad received the Royal assent or appeared in the Gazette, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer in tparicular is said to have felt highly offenaed at this violation of etiquette. But tbe cat is out and the Commission will sit ; how long is another ques-

don. It may be for years, if certain pessimists do not in the meantime become too thoroughly alarmed to allow members to proceed in the solemn and deliberative way which usually characterises Royal Commissions. Be that as it may an authori- tative pronouncement on the question of the national coal supply will be received when it comes by the majority of people throughout the country with all the respect which it certainly deserves.

The Child Messenger Act appears to have excited a most unusual commotion among publicans and their outdoor customers. The Act, as by this time everybody has been made to know, came into operation on New Year's Day, and already a conflict or opinion, not only as to the prospects of its efficacy, but in regard to the proper interpretation of its provisions, has arisen in various parts of the provinces. The chairman of the Worcestershire quarter sessions holds that the use of a gummed slip round the cork of a bottle woul I not comply with the law which demands a "sealed vessel." The majority of "the trade" had come to the con- clusion that the employment of the gummed slip would suffice. Some critics are of opinion that the Act was intended to mean that the bottles should be corked and sealed on the premises when the drink was purchased, and not that empty bottles, jars, and cans should be taken to licensed houses to be refilled. But this is only one aspect of the new statute that has within the past three or four days challenged attention. There are cer- tain others, and among them the question of deter- mining the age of the youthful Ganymede. A spacial commissioner who has been making inquiries in London, wrote to an evening paper this week pointing out that police officers of experience are not favourably impressed with the Act, although, like the temperance party, they express an opinion that it is a step in the right direction and may be amended if found essentially defective in opera- tion. There is good sense in all this, and if police officers of great experience were to let us know what they consider would be the best way of secur- ing the object for which the Act was passed, the general public, as distinguishe 1 from the landlord and his customers only, might have reason to feel satisfied. For, as matters stand, it is more than likely that: the proverbial " coach-and-six," first alluded to by John Bright, will be continually run- ning through the newly enacted statute. But, again, what are people who manage to live well and comfortably without troubling the publican at all, to think of an article that the concentrated wisdom of the people, as represented in Parliament has decided to hedge about with so many restric- tions and precautionary measures as all this means?

SUDDEN DEATH OF AN OLD WOMAN. At the Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday after- noon an inquest. was held touching the death of Rose Scott, marine store dealer Heath-road, aged 59 years.--The evidence showed that ths deceased had gone to the house ot her married daughter's Elizabeth Ann Hough, on Saturday slightly under the influence of drink. She slept on the sofa from 3f inthteh he oauf st afternoon rrneot returned r night. At that time 0 o;23ed and at the oacupants t 3.45 next morning she was found dead by her nd until t 1 a daughter. The medical evidence showed that death was due to fatty degeneration that the lungs and liver were in a pulpy condition, and that there was a hole at the back of the stomach. —A verdict in accordance with the medical evidence was re- turned.

At most of the places of worship on New Year's eve watchnight services were held before fair con- gregations. At 12 o'clock the streets were crowded to witness the incoming of the New Year. div.head: RUNCORN NOTES. [BY A CORRESPONDENT.)
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES. [BY A CORRESPONDENT.)

Thursday's Urban Council meeting must be almost a record one in despatching of public busi- ness. It lasted under ten minutes, and proves what a distinctly happy family is this authority. What a pity this much cannot be said about otner local authbrities not far distant ! Practically but routine business was done, but it is worthy of nate that the Council have decided to issue the advertisement and posters which, a recent finding of magistrates has made necessary in order to proceed against anyone guilty of private slaughtering.

The decoration of the Council Chamber is now complete and very sober yet artistic it looks. The photographs of late Chairmen of the Council have been mounted in suitable frames and are placed round the wall while over the mantel piece the photograph of Q aeon Victoria hangs in a suitable overmantel. Mr Wilding, who bas supervised the entire scheme deserves a word of praise for his excellent work.
There Wa3 little bu.iness at the Board of Guardians and the Rural Council on Tuesday. The only important item was the resolution whio again referred the water question to the Runcorn Uroan Council.

The New Year was ushered in at Runcorn in a very quiet way. A continuous drizzle of rain wit- nessed the departure of the old year and the birth of the new. The crowds were not very numerous and there was an utter aboence of rowdyism. The town now appears to be almost lifeless and every- body is waiting for the spring to bring the prosper- ity and happiness which one wishes to eaca other on New Year's day.

In connection with the Methodist million scheme Runcorn, with the whole of the Methodist connec- tion:held a joint collection on Sunday throughout the circuit. It is satisfactory to note that the handsome sum of £7O was received and it is inter- esting to know that on Tuesday a cheque for £2.70 was sent to the general fund. This makes a con- tribution from the circuit, exclusive of the collec- tion, of £1.600 leaving £BO to complete the 1,600 guineas promised.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Successive defeats by fladdersfleld, Widnes and Warrington had made Runcorn people begin to wonder whether their team was on the down-grade. Until Warrington did the trick on Boxing Day, Runcorn had never suffered a reverse on their own ground in a League fixture for three years, and the Wire-pullers performance was the unkindest cut of I all. As a consequence, confidence in the ability of , the team to capture two points at the expense of Salford on Satuiday was not very pronounced at all, and the general feeling was reflected in the poor support the match received. The Reds were expec- ted to be a big draw ; but as a matter of fact there were barely five hundred people present. And the miserable weather will not wholly account for the lamentable slump in the " gate." If "nothing succeeds like success," the converse would seem to equally apply that "Nothing fails like failure." The Warrington match realised £l2B, the Salford match would scarcely bring in the odd I:2B,and it is regrettable that a few reverses should eause the team to lack popular support in this fashion. It is not sports- manlike to refuse to hold out the helping hand(and shouting voice) in the hour of adversity. And everybody knows the club is 1103 e too ric a for the position it has to maintain.

But to the match. Neither team was at full strength. Salford were short of Tom Williams and Tanney and of the home team Houghton, Faulkner and Farmer were absent. The frost and the heavy rains had converted the ground for a considerable portion of its length into a mud paddle and natur- ally was not conducive to a scientific exposition of the game. Runcorn have earned a 1:111038 for the kick and rush style of play but this seemed the proper thing under the circumstances and both sides indulged in it emnewhat freely. Here Run- corn held one advantage that they fielded the ball more cleanly than their opponents and as the home forwards followed up persistently and untiringly to the finish they regained that reputation for smartness which has been somewhat besmirched of late.

--- It was a lively well contested game from start to finish but Runcorn were decidedly the best team In the scrummages and on the loose the Salford forwards were inferior to the R.uncoro eight, an the display of the Salford back!, under the circum- stances merits unstinted praise. Smith had Plenty ot work and seldom was he at fault. He fielded, kicked and tackled in his best style and he was well supported in his defence by Oriffi:hs and Lomas, the lialf-backs, who played a flue uphill game. Price was distinctly the best of the three- quarters, and put in several highly meritorious runs. Bone was seldom in an aggres- sive mood and consequently was never dangerous. He seemed to have a difficulty in showing his paces when he did receive the ball. Varty played a sound gam.. Of the forwards Brown was very conspicuous, but probably the best work was done by Worthington,Rhapps and Shore. Furnival, who did duty for liou.zhton on the Run- corn side, is a youngster who has only been with the club a few weeks. He made a craditab'e show that gave promise of better thin,qs when he gets settled down. He played with grit which is a good founlation for a fullback, and his kicking taken all round was very strong and clear. It was pleasing to see the Runcorn three-quarters have a chance to show their passing skill nod each try was the result of a good movement. Butterworth was in first rate form and Moran showed what he can do when he gets the chance. Wilkin- son did some fine defensive work that mate Bone' harmless. As usually Jolley was "all over the shop " doing an immense amount of work, and be opened oat the passing effectively on several occa- sions. Of a splendid set of forwards Walker, Moulton and Woods may he singled out for mention.

The game with I-full was a very fine one 01 New Year's day. The Linaets shaped exceptionally well and many think that they have sellorn displayed finer form. Be that as i. may Runcorn showed uo smartly and were equatly glad on the Ctack on ths defence. Hui', ira fact, were completely de- moralized during the earlier portion of the game and but for wakening up in the nick of time a most crushing defeat would have been recorded against them.

The Greens were muoh waperior fore and aft to their oppanents and it is kicky far Hull that Houghton was a hit off colour owing to hi i rec•ent illness. Taylor played a maznific...en; game far the visitors and avdd the side over and over again. He was, indeed,the on!y nasn who shone at all on their side.

All the Malcom threequarers vlayea with judw,- mem there being' a capital understanding between the backs. Moran came out strongly at times and gave a very neat display. Jo!ley played a fine game at half back while Walker at forward was to the fore through° i. Naturally there is at present joy , in the Runcorn camp.
A TERROR TO TOWNS UND,-ASSSULTS ON Two POLICE CONSTABLES AND A PUBLIC HOUSE MANAGER

At thweVa-rr-17r:O.J.Police Court on Thursday before Dr White (in the chair) and Mr Henherd Ralph Taylor was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Pinners-brsw the previous evening, refusing to quit the " Lord Rodney " Inn when requested to do so, and also with assaulting John Glover, the manager of the public-house and Police Con- stables Wise and Taylor.—John Glover atatei that at 6 10 the previous evening prisoner canoe into the publ:c. house drunk and ordered a drink. Witness knew the man and owing to his previous conduct and character and to his condition he refusal to serve him. He asked him to go out but prisoner zefused to do so and witness went, to the door to see if he could see a police of 6 3er. When he returned prisoner was "making a bother" in the house, having picked up another man's glass of beer. When witness went to him prisoner rushed at him and butted him with his head, , tie also tried to bite him and struck him in the eye. P.C. Wise came upon the scene but could do nothing mith the man, who knocked him about and kicked bim.The assistance of P.O. Taylor was obtained and both OffiCerd had to struggle on the ground with the prisoner, who was ultimately taken to the Police Station.—P 0 Wise said the prisoner was very violent and kicked witness on the leg and struck him. He also kicked PC Taylor and they were obliged to handcuff him.—P C Taylor corroborated and stated that owing to their struggling on the ground the uniforms of P C Wise and himself wore covered with mud. -Superintendent Monagoan said he had known prisoner for twenty years. He .bad been convicted 12 times at Warrington, having been imprisoned for assaulting the police A. long list of con- victions had also been received from the St Helens police, and the man had been convicted at Melton Mowbray. lie never worked and was a terror to towns-end when he Came to Warrington.—Prisorter,who stated that be was drunk and did not know what be was doing, was sent to gaol for four m ontbs,

div.p: HEALTH COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended that the followicg in- structions be given to the Sanitary Inspector : That he be in attendance in his office at the Town Hall from nine to ten o'clock in the I/amnia:a, and from two to three o'clock in the afternoons, and that these hours be indicated on the door: that he 111113 t pay at least three visits a week to the slaughter-houses,and that be record and report monthly to the Health C =matte as to these inspections; that he must visit the hospital three times a week whenever there is a patient or patints therein,and once • week when the hospital is vacant, and that he record and report his visits once a month to the Health Committee ; that infected houses be disinfected by the Council free of cost with the consent of the owner or owners,and that the Sanitary Inspector report monthly to the Health Committee as to the houscs disinfected, giving date of disinfection and situation of premises. Confirmed on the proposition of Messrs Jones and Handley.

div.head: WINWICK ASYLUM.
div.p: WINWICK ASYLUM.
THE SEWAGE QUESTION.

LETTER TO THE BEY CaNON PENRRYN. At a meeting of the Warrington Rural District. Council held on ‘Vednesday the Clerk (Mr J C Sutton) reported that he had addressed the following letter to the Rev Canon Penrhyu, chairman of the Wiuwick Parish Coun- cil, respecting the disposal of the Asylum sewage : Dear sir,—The Clerk of Win wick Parish Council desires an 2xplanatlon to be given you, as Chairman of that Council, upon the differences existing re the rem oval of sewage from the New Winwick Asylum. I may first say that the Rural District Council is " the Local Authority," and that the Winwick parish is a " separate Sewerage District chargeable with all sewer expenses falling upon the Local Authority in respect ot sewerage works at Winwick. The Lan- cashire Asylums Board represent, a ratable value of over twenty:two millions stirliug. In whatever exceptional instance it may not be wholly so, their Asylums sewerage system is generally provided for from the fund used for asylum buildings, hence it was that the plans of the New Win wick Asylum included a system for dis- posal of the asylum sewage. Upon first occupation of Winwick Hall the Asylums Board was assessed on the old assessment, and so paid the small proportion of a , special rate of twopence in the £ levied on the parish to provide a sower suffieient for the few housss along the Winwick-road. including the two lodges and a new residence upon the land of the Winwick asylum Estate. The discharge from this sewer would for many years to come he slight. Toe Parish Council and the Local Authority distinct y understood at this period, and indead until the great Asylum buildings were very tar advanced, that the Asylums Board would pro r:de for disposal of Asylum sewage. It is said thee actually borrowed, or had auth- ority to borrow, £lO,OOO for the purpose. Meeting, it is presumed, with some great difficulty, they invited this Authority to a conference in Januar, last with their Board and the Warrington Corporation. It see:nel to this Authority that having regard to the already sad condition of Sankey Brook, once a pure and valuable stream, and to commencement of remedies now being forced upon St Helens, a great engineering sewerage scheme, involving great first and continual cost, is con- templated, and that upon co, nection of their drainage system with the local sewer the Asylums Board will be relieved of responsibility, and the parish will have an 'order enforced upon, them which the inhabitants will be ill able to bear. It is to be remembered that the inhabitants of Winwick are charged with their portion of the cost of the sewage sestemlat Rainhill and other asylums, and that the over 2,000 lunatics to be brought to and maintained at the asylum are, in the eyes the law, inhabitants of the parishes at which they are settled or of the districts from which they have been removed. The Asylums Beard are forbidden to make use of the lola' sewer. They will find it difficull, if they drs-egard the action of the local authority, to connect their drainage system with the sewer, unless they secure a right of laying sewer pipes in lands of the ecclesiastical commissioners This right we havejrecently learned they are seeking, and it is properties commissioners ought to be informed of the consequences thereof in respect of the tuture fall in the value of their lands, of the increase of the local rates, and of the effect upon the health of the district. Grant of the easement ought in any Cade to he deferred until the matters explained have rece.ved careful con- sideration byPthe commissioners. The Local Authority will concur with an equitable adjustment whereby the ' erection of the asylum will not fix upon them immeasur- able responsibility or inequitable additional local burdens.—Yours faithfully, J C Surros, Clerk to the Rural District Council. The CLERK also submitted further correspondence with Mr T P Muspratt, clerk to the Asylums Visiting Committee of the Lancashire County Council, and Mr W D Jeans, who has been instructed to act for toe Council, in the event of Btigation,had an interview with the Council. The proceeding were strietly private.

BURTONWO^D WATER SUPPLY-OPP3SITION TO TILE PROPOSED EXTENSION.

A leer wan received from the Clerk to the Button- wood Parish Council (Mr John Fairclough) stating that at a recent meeting of ratepayers the following resolu- tion was passed That the Buttonwood water main be extended on the terms proposed in the letter dated 27th November from the Town Clerk of Warrington to the Clerk of :be Warrington Rural District Coutcil and that the said terms be and are hereby accented." The CHAIRMAN said he had received the following letter, signed by Mr John Warburton and five other I ratepayers..—"We, the undersigned ratepayers,berewitb bee to protest against the extension of the water scheme. At a meeting held on Monday last we were only defcated by six votes which we thiols is not a fair representation required to extend such an expensive undertaking. We trust you will postpone the business until such a time as the Corporation can see their way clear to reduce the percentage." Mr Fogsnew said there were only twenty persona present at the meeting and thirteen voted for the resolu- tion. He would give notice that at the next meeting he would move a reJolution that the terms of the Corpura- tion be accepted in aceordance with the recommenda- tion of the parish meeting. Mr HALTON thought that a better way out of the difficulty would be to get the landlords who requited I the water: to give the guarantee for the percentage, as they had done at Sankey. It would be a hardship for ratepayers who obtained no benefit from the undertak- ing to contribute towards the cost. It was a most serious thine for the Council to sanction. Mr HOUGHTON said that he was one of three on the Manchester-road who gave a guarantee in the way moo- tinned by Mrs Halton. Mr FORMAT: said they could not get the landlords who bad already been supplied with water to forego that advantage and guarantee the percentage. The matter then dropped. THE COLOURING OF SWEETS.

The INSPECTOR reportedlhat in consequewo of a COM • plaint made to bim af the doubtful puri:y of sweets sold to children in ore of the t mnships,he purchased a sam- ple and sent it to Dr Cut H. Bell for analysis, and he reported thereon as follows : I have tested the samrlz of sweets, and I find that the yellow colour is due to vegetable matter and not to chromate of lea tas far as I can see the sweets are pure, but lam making further experiments."

THE VULCAN BRIDGE. The SURVEYOR informed the Council that as instruc- ted at the last mewing, he had now examined the Vulcan Bridge carefully, and begged to report thereon as follows :—(a) That the arch is pfrfeCtly sound and has not at a.ly time been disturbed sines construction, and it is quite strong enough to carry the present ordinary traffic of the district. () That at some time heavy traffic has bulged and strained the retaining wall on the Earlestown side of the bridge, which should be shored up and reoairad, but which does not affect the carrying strength of the bridge. This has been caused through icsufficient concrete b.cicing to the arch in con- struction. (c) The Warrington side retaining walla are sound enough for the necessity of the present time. The report was adopted.

Funeral of the Late Mr. G. F. Plumpton. The remains of the late Mr G F Plumpton (whose sad death was reported in our last issue) were laid to rest at Sankey Cemetery on Sunday afternoon in the presence of a very large number of mourners, friends, and those who had been fellow-sportsmen with the deceased. The last solemn and impressive rites wereponducted by the Rev I R Jones,vicar of Sankey. The body was borne to its last resting place by bearers who numbered themselves amongst his friends and associates in the Widnes Football Club. namely, Messrs Wright, Aspey,liem- ingway, Laws, Smith, Foster, Minton, and Farrell. Noticeable among the wreaths was a beautiful floral token sent by the Widnes Club, which was carried at the head of the funeral cortege by Messrs A Alforde and F Murphy. Among the mourners were also a large number of the Wallington friends , of the deceased footballer.

div.head: LICENSING PROSECUTION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: LICENSING PROSECUTION AT RUNCORN.
Case Dismissed.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, William Baker, landlord of the " Grapes Inn," Halton-road. was summoned for selling liquor to drunken per- sons, to wit, James Sheeri and Joseph Cliff a un the 14th December.—Mr Fletcher (Northvvicb) appeared on behalf of the police, and Mr A Tobin, barrister. (Liverpool), instructed by Mr F A Lake, solicitor, appeared for the defendant. Mr. J R Frith, manager of Runcorn Gas Works, stated that on the 14th December the men Sheen and Cliffe should have come to work. In conse- quence of their absence he went to look for them at 12.30. He called a constable and they went to the" Grapes Inn" and found tbe men there. Both were drunk. He had not the slightest doubt about it.—Cross-examined by Mr Tobin t They were not at all offensive in their behsviour and he judged they were drunk before triey spoke to him. He could tell by their eyes. Henry Nield foreman at the Gas Works, corroborated the fact that the men were drunk.

In reply to Mr Tobin he said that the ;;;;;;ere far on in drink but he would not say positively they were drunk because ii, all hinged on the definition of drunkenness. P.C. Davies depobed that the men were think when he went in with Mr Frith. They were not quarrelsome and he would not have arrested them.—By the Bench If he had met them in the street he would have known they were drunk but wou:d not twre arrested them as they were quiet. Mr Tobin, for the d fence, contended that the men were not drunk and that Messrs Frith and Nield could mt say positively whether they were drunk or not be- cause they were vexed at their non-attendance at work. They could not be impartial._ _ _ . _
Florence Jane Baker, wife of the defendant, aad they had kept the house for s'a years and had never had a complaint about the management. Her husband was not in at the tirn^. The men were not drunk.

Joseph filiffe deposed that on that date he was.sene to Sham's house at 8.45 for him to go to work. They made it up to go ratting instead. They went to wit- ness's house for his ferret and called at the "Dog and Partridge "and had one pint of beer. They then went to the " Gear e "on the way for Sheen's ferret and callei for two whiskeys. He only had one pint of beer that day and left the whiskeys on the table when Mr Frith came in. • William Sheen corrobotat.d.
Mns Dizibeth Shaw, sister of Cliff, Mrs Field, and William Ackerly corroborats.l teat ttie men were not drunk
The case was dismissed on the ground of insufficient evidence.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES

--- - A CHRISTMAS EVE INCIDENT AT A PUBLIC HOUSE. At the Warrington Police Court yesterday before Conn- cillor Smethurst and other magistrates George Moxey 3. Lees yard, off Haydock-street was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick street at 10.45 on Tuesday evening and also with being drank on the licensed premises of Mr Joseph Shillcock. .• Bay Horse" Inn. Winwick-street, and refusing to quit when requested to de so—Mr Browne appeared on behalf of the prosecutor and said that the de- fendant and two women came into the" Bay Horse" Inn. Winwick-street, on Tuesday night. They were all very drunk. Mrs Shilicoek was behind the bar and she refused to serve them and requested them to leave. They made use of horribly filthy language and defendant began to fight with another customer. The cus- tomers put him out and matters went on quietly until 1030, when defendant returned not only with the women but with another man named Flynn. It appeared that the two women were the wives of the men. Mr sileillcock ordered them out but they refused to go and again made use of bad language. Mr Shillcock tried to put them out but he could not and ' Flynn tore his collar. When the customers saw Mr Shin rook being used in this manner they sent to his assistance and the defendant was put out. The police were sent for the house being in an uproar. Sergeant Barnett arprehended defendant in the street and he refused to give his, name. He was taken to the Police Station but was bailed out on Christmas morning.—Mr Sbillcock desired it to be known that these people were not customers at his house. He had previously refused to serve the defendant on account of his conduct.—A fine of lOs and costs was imposed. A PAWNER'RER SUMMONED AT WARRING/nen. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. er Monks and other magistrates, Benjamin Love, pawn- broker, Dial-street. was summoned for having on December leth taken a pair of trousers in pawn from a child under twelve years of age.—Mr. Browne appeared for the defend- ant.—The Chief Constable said the prosecution was the first of its kind whieli had taken place in Warrington for BOMB years. It appeared that a man named John Nicholson. a slater living at 68. Ellesmere-street, had a son aged eight years, wbo was a very bad little boy for his age. On the 18th of December Mr Nicholson missed a pair of trousers from a bedroom and in consequence of inquiries he made he went to the defendant's shop and saw Mrs Love. He asked her if she remembered taking a pair of trousers in pledge frosts the boy and she replied " I think I do." Information was given to the police as Nicholson felt very strongly in the matter. The boy pawned the trousers without any difneulty, tore up the ticket and spent the money which he obtained for them Ininepencen Superintendent Monegban and Detective Foreter visited the shop on December 24th and Mrs Love admitted having received the trousers, and added that they were in the habit of taking things in pledge from boys of Nicholson" age —For the defence Mr Browne did not dis- pute the facts but said that the boy told Mrs Love that his father had sent him with the trousers. The outside profit which the defendant would make on the transaction was a half penny and for such a paltry amount it was not worth breaking the law. Mr Love had a large notice in his shop stating that pledges would not be taken from children and he denied that he had been in the hebit 0' taking pledges from boys so young as Nicholson.— The Otte! Constable pointed out that it was such conduct as this that made young thieves.—The Chairman said the Bench ,d 'toe oppn -na test tO , 04 B Wii ea off en e against the law and it was desirable that pawnbrokers should keep , within the law. Under the eircumstences, however, they would dismiss defendant with a caution, on his paying the costs of the semmons. SEonnteto HOME LIFE—A NEGLIGENT MOTHER SENT T) PRISON. Fophia Madigan, a widow residing at 34, Bettersby-lane, Warrington, was brought up at the County Borough Police Court on Tuesday and charged with neglecting her two chil- dren in a mannenlikely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health-311e pleaded guilty—Mr Browne pro- secuted on bebalttof the:N S.P.C.C. andisaid that the children Thomas and Johnwere aged eight years and eight months respectively4Tbe baby aged eight months insteed of welghing 1410. the normal weight, weighed only 7lbs. The house was in a most shocking condition, in fact this was about the worst case he (Br Browne) had apeeared in. Inspector .nlackett had had the woman under observation for some months. He visited the house on Monday and found the bov Thomas WAS poorly nourished and poorly clad. His body was very dirty and the skin was broicen. The child John was naked, being wrapped in a small rug. and WISS very emaciated and dirty. The bedding in the house was in a most horrible condition. When charged with the offence prisoner replied : "It is true. It's no use saying anything, at the thing speaks for itself." The woman had teen drinking every day and was hardly ever sober.—Dr Bowden gave evidence and said the neglect mutt have been very bad.—Prisoner said the baby Ind suffered from eon- sumption.—She was sent to gaol for three months with hard labour. THEFT BY A WARRINGTON SERVANT. At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Mr. Long (in the chair) and other magistrates, a yoeng woman named Annie Bond, who lives atl9, Mill-lane, Warrington, was charged with having stolen a diamond ring of the value of fourteen guineas, from/ the house of Mrs. Mary Al:ce Mason. 19, iellesmere-road. liitocktnn Heath, on or about Deoember 21st —Prisoner pleaded guilty—Mrs. Mason said the woman came to her as a servant on Thursday, December 19th. On the following Saturday evening about eight o'clock prisoner left the house, saying she was going to bring her boxet. When she returned she said her mother had met with an accident, and as she felt uneasy, she wished to leave and go borne. Tole accident had occurred she Bald when the mother was help:ng her to get her boxes downstairs. Witness missed the ring about five o'clock on Saturday afternoon. It had been In a jewel case and was worth fourteen guineas.— Evan Evans, manager hr Mr Thomas Dornville,pawnbroker, Priestley.street, Warringtonnsaid that on December 21st the nrisoner came to the shop and offered a diamond ring in pledge. She asked for El on it and said it belonged to her parents. Sloe gave her name as Annie Bond, 18, Mill-street, and was fashionably dressed. This and the fact that the family were customers, mule him come to the Conclusion that it was all right—P.C. Tart deposed to having received information of the theft and said he apprehended prisoner MI the 24th at the house of her parents. He Made inquiries and subsequently recovered the ring from Mr Domville's stop —The magistrates considered thet the kindest thing for them to do was to commit prisoner to goal for a Month. There her mental condition would be inquired into ; and if anything was ong It would Le recognized.—Mrs Bond, w.r mother of the prisoner. said her daughter Wes occasionally not responsible for her actions.

Prisoner followed him and withoat the slightest provocation struck him twice in the stomach and ribs. He afterwards " came for him again " and struck him. Prisoner then be- came very violent and struggled with witness for some time. Witness took him into emit° ty and on being asked what he had committed the assault for he replied ; "I wanted to be locked up. I wanted a night's lodging." At the Police Station prisoner again and again attempted to strike him.—The Chief Constable said the man admitted having been locked up before for assaulting the police. It was a favourite pastime of his when he was in his "cups."—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. ImPonEstY .2ERFT.—Thomas Warburton. 64, Sharp-street, was charged with having stolen a man's corduroy jacket, value 34 63 from the shop of unsworth Brothers, in Lyme- street, at six o'clock on Saturday night.—The Chief Con- stable stated that at the time in question P.C. Sankey was on duty in the district, and saw the prisoner go into the doorway and pick up a corduroy jacket. He put it under his coat and walked away. Sankey caught him, and took him back to the shop, where thi jacket was identlEed as the firm's property. The man, having no alternative, admitted the theft. He was a pe•sistent slsop-door thief.—The magis- trates sent him to gaol for a month. THE CHRISTMAS EVE SCENE AT A PUBLIC•HOVSE.—Thomas Glynn and Mary Glynn. 37, Watkin-street, and Eliza Moxey. 3. Lees-yard. were summoned for being drunk on the licensed premises of Mr. Joseph Shillcoek, "Bay Horse " Winwlck-street, and refusing to quit when requested to do so on December 24th.—Mr Browne appeared for the prosecutor, and stated that on Christmas Eve a man named Moxey, who was dealt with last Friday morning, came Into the public-house in com- pany with the female defendants. All three were very drunk and Mrs Shilleock refused to serve them. They were sent out,but at 10.30 returned accompanied by the man Glynn. Mr Shillcock ordered them out but they refused to go and he bad to eject them with the assistance of some customers. Defendants made use of horrible language.— Evidence having been given, defendants were each fined s and costs. A DISORDERIY WOMAN, -Ada Dixon, 20 Thelwall-lane, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in linutsford-road on the 23rd Deeernber.—P.C. Cooper stated that at eleven o'clock lon the Monday evening named he was on duty near the place in question, when he saw the defendant near a cabin. She was drunk and had a bottle of whisky. He requested her to go home, and she struck him in the face. She was screaming and shouting and refused to go home, using bad language.—Sergeant Evans said that he saw the defendsnt in Thelssall-lane later on and she was drunk and very abusive—Defendant said she was called over to the cabin by some friends who wanted to know about a bother which had taken place, and as she did not wish to be seen by the constable, she" just slipped Into the cabin."— She was fined ss.

Appli- cant stated that one of his children had been seriously ill through being vaccinated, and that if children ought to be vaccinated he believed that the Creator would have vaccinated them before they were born.—After a passage of arms between the applicant and the chairman the application WA granted. I WizoLESALE THEFTS.—Henry Lowe and Patrick 'Grady were charged with havir.g stolen a half pint and a pint pewter pat valued at 5s 70 belonging to Catherine Warder, landlady of the "Rose and Crovrn."—Grady was also charged with having stolen a bottle of whiskey from William Baker licensee of the " Grapes Inn " Halton-road, on the 23rd December. He was further charged with having stolen an overcoat valued at 15s. the property of Thomas Clarke farmer, Norton. on the same day. After evidence had been given proving that the prisoner had committed the felonies the magistrate committed Lowe to prison for 14 days and Grady for one month in each case to run con- secutively. div.head: WESLEYAN MILLION GUINEAS FUND. -- Special Effort.
div.p: THE WESLEYAN MILLION GUINEAS FUND. -- Special Effort.

A special effort was mad& on Sunday throughout the Wesleyan Methodist Church to complete the Million Guineas Twentieth Century Fund. The idea of Ite fund was started three or four years ago by Mr ft W , Perks, M.P., who is the acting treasurer, and it has , been taken up with much zest throughout British Methodism, although an influential few have held aloof from the movement. At first it. was proposed to secure a million guineas by the time the new century was entered upon, but as this was found impracticable there was a general agreement to extend the time for the redemption of promises to the close of the present year. Before Sunday's collections the report was that £900,000 had been promised, and £700,000 had been actually paid. Over a hundred thousand guineas tberefore remained to be rahed. Collections were made en Sunday in ad the Wesleyan churches and schools, and at each collection new promises as well as money gifts were invited. The objects of the fund are as follow i—E.300,000 for the erection end enlargemen; of chapels, Sunday schools, manses, soldiers' and sailors' homes, ‘S.:z ; £200,000 for educational work, £lOO,OOO for foreign missions, £lOO,OOO for home missions and temperance work, £50,000 for the Chil- dren's Home, and £250,000 for a central hall in London. _ .

• Collections were taken at all Wesleyan places of wor- ship in Warrington on Sunday on behalf of the fund. Toe services at Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel were largely attended and of a very hearty description. The preacher in the morning was the Rev W C J Neville, who spoke from Joel, ii. 21. In the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev 1 Bishop who took as his subject" Great Expectations." Bespoke of the present time as one ot the great things, huge trusts, vast railways, immense ateamboats,co-operative societies, and sther huge con- cerns. Referring to the present effort be said that Metho- dism was to be put on a firmer basis and to have more capital. The hymns sung during the day were exactly the same and to the same tune as those sung in all the Wesleyan Methodist places of worship throughout the United Kingdom, and were very feelingly reacered. At the Padgate Wesleyan Chnrch, on Sunday, special ser- mons were preached morning and evening by the Rev H Valentine. In the afternoon a chi!dren's service was held, when Mr Arthur Bennett gave an address. Spec' al hymns were sung at each service. The follow- ing list gives the amount of tne collecthns taken in the Warrington Circuit :—Bold-•treet Chapel, £32 03 2d : Bewsey-road, £l2 5s ; Sankey Bridges. £3 13s 51 ; Latchford, £4 10s 6d ; Ellesmere-street, £1 161 3d ; Buttock-street. 2s 6d ; 1.9111 M, £4 5s ii ; Penketh, £5O; Moore, £l4 6s 81 ; Wbitley. £1 03 2el ; Antrobus, £1 12s ; Appleton', £2 is 2d ; Padgate, £5O ; Hatton, 84 7 Martinscrolt, £1 is; and Stockton Heath, £2 ls 3d; represettmg a grand total of £lBl 34 Ed.
