div.head: WARRINGIOE BADLY ATRN BY BRADFORD.
div.p: WARRINGIOE BADLY ATRN BY BRADFORD.

The Park Avenue men came to Warrington on Wednesday with a full team and found the home side short of Hallam, full back; Townson, half back ; and Morrison and Fell, for- wards. There was a fine crowd of some 6.00) people the weather being a considerable improvement on the sort which had prevailed during previous matches. Mr J ti Barker of Liversedge was the referee an I the teams lined out as follows Warrington : Ratcliffe, full back ; Fish, leherwood, Dickenson and Harris, three-quarters ; Burgess and Hocken- hall, half backs ; Taylor, Boardman, Edmondson, J Swift, W Swift, W Ashton, Cunningham and Eden, forwards. Bradford : Mosby, full back ; Pollard, Etagere, Mare- troyd and Wilson, three-quarters ; Marsden ain.t Heseltine, half-backs ; Smedley, Hutt, Feather, Wright, Lsidlow, Smailes, Dean and Robertson, forwards. Warrington losing the toss, J Swift started against the wind and Broadley returned. Early on the Bradfordians forced matters and Marsden passing Out, Murgatroyd and Wilson made progress on the left until Harris brought down the latter. Hockenhall relieved somewhat by a prompt tackle of Marsden, but the visitcrs came down smartly once more and Dickenson saved pluckily near the line' Warring- ton were overweighted and overplayed.but defended well. For standing otLide Harris was penalised and Mosby missed an easy goal-kick. Bradford kept up the attack eau Pollard ran over at the corner from alaraden's pass, Fish making a feeble effort to shove him in touch. Give and take play followed, but Bradford were very persistent and Isherwood saved on the line Wilson was again brought down by Harris. Bradford scrimmaged close in end Burgess broke away, finely passing to Fieh at the quarter flag. The wing man took the ball beautifully and outpacing Pollard scored In good position after a brilliant effort. Ratcliffe failed at goal. Warrington played up now, Isherwood, Burgess and Fish coming very near penetrating the visitors defence again. Fish only just missed a penalty goal. A mull by Ratcliffe gave Bradford footing in the Warrington iaalf again, and the referee allowed them two kicks out of touch when close to the line. From the second Heseltine got over under the posts and Eagan kicked a goal. Half-time : Bradford, eight points ; Warrington, three points. Broadley restarted, and by the aid of free kicks Bradford got into the Warrington half scam. Ratcliffe was at fault and Hockenhall also mulliog Marsden got a scrambling sort of try in the first five minutes. Mosby failing at goal. Warrington showed poor form, while their opponents Improved every minute. Fish only just robbed Pollard at the corner. Burgess wee the means of Warrington attacking again, and for a short time the home men made great efforts, which were rewarded by a penalty goal from the foot of Fish. 'Bradford dashed up the field again and Heseltine was injured, Broadley coming out of the pick in his place. The Bradford skipper git hold near the line, and brushing Ratcliffe aside scoeed easily, Eggers placing a goal. War- rington responded with another rush, and smart passing should have resulted in a try but Dicken- son was at fault. Broadley was soon in evidence again, and by a magnificent dribble from the centre scored near the pos's, but the referee disallowed the point. Mnrgatroyd and Wilson made a fine run on the left,but Rat- cliffe knocked the wing man in touch. Fast play followed and the visitors forwards taking up the running Broadley romped over again, Eagers missing the goal. Warrington were quite oat-classed but showed grit in the closing stages ' After Harris and Hockenhall had failed to get in. Fish picked up smartly and dodging the Bradford men in his own par- ticular style scored cleverly near the corner, and only missed converting by inches' The end came next minute, the score reading: Bradford 2 goals, 5 tries (19 points) ; Warrington 1 goal, 2 tries (8 points.) RUNCORN V. HULL.

This fixture was p'aytd at Runcorn on New Year's Day before an attendance of about 2,000. The teams were fairly representative. Houghton taking his accustomed place at full back for Runcorn. Langley started for Runcorn against a stiff breeze and after a little de‘ultory play the game settled in the visitors' 25. Two minutes from the start Jolley obtained possession and threw to Butterworth who in turn handed to Warder who, after a brilliant run scored. Moulton failed to augment. Richardson neirly got through bit was grassed on the line. Run- corn still maintained the peessure and after a fine round of passing between the home backs Moran scored between the posts. Moulton still further improved the point. A break- away by the Hull front rank placed. Runcorn on the defence but the Runcorn backs again getting possession carried the leather to the visitors' lines. Butterworth scoring after running the length of the field with the entire pace after him. The visitors' backs were now Been to a little better advantage ; Runcorn. however, maintained a fine defence which Hall could not pierce. Repeated scrummages left the advantage with Runcorn. play settling at midfield. The visitors were now combining much better, a passing move- ment by the home backs being nipped in the bud. Taylor robbed Richardson when a score was imminent and a mo- ment later Ritson got the ball at his toes, and, with a tine dribble, scared between the posts, Jacques improvieg.—Run- corn had several good opportunities after this but could not rise to the occasion. Wilkinson was grassed on the line and Warder had a futile drop at goal. Brilliant play by Taylor saved his side repeatedly. A hot attack on the visitors' line came to naught owing to the fine defence. Holt arrived with Runcorn leaving by one goal three tries to Hull one goal one try. At the change of ends Hull placed with vigour placing Runcorn OR the defence. Each end was visited in turn the game becoming fast and open. Repeated Scrums took the leather to the visitors line where a score was but narrowly averted. Moran Jolley and Butterworth initiated a movement but the latter player was collared. Taylor kicked well, collaring his mire, Runcorn failing to make any impression. Miller was hurt temporarily and during his absence Jolley made a capital run and kick, from which Williams picked up and score.l the goal kick failing. Ritson had to retire hurt. Runcorn continued to display excellent com- bination keeping the play well within their Opponents 25. A fine break away was spoiled by Taylor kicking dead Just before time Butterworth cored. Final: Runcorn. 2 goals 5 tries ; Hull, 1 goal 1. try.
BROUGHTON BANGERS '7 BATLEY.

The return match between these Cill3ll was played on the Rangers ground on Wednesday. before about 8,000 specta- tors. Both clubs were otr ongly represented, and a well- contested game was witnessed, which the Rangers won by the narrow margin of two pliota. The chief feature of the game was the splendid defence which the Batley backs cffered to the continual attacks by the Rangetn, as they were playing behind a beaten set of forward 4 throughout. It was only by W James kicking two goals that the Rangers were able to first draw level and finally win the match. Final /more —Broughton Rangers, two goals and one try (seven points) ; Batley, one goal and one try (five points),

EICRLESTOWN V. WARRING,TON. These teams met at Barleatown on Saturday, the ground being in very bad condition. Barlestown played the same team that beat Kaydock by six goals to ni on Thursday,

while Warrington were well represented. Wariington layed up-hill with the wind in the first half. Operations were commenced by Dawson. Riley was early prominent I for the visitors. but Was fouled, and nothing tangible re- sulted. For a short time Warrington pressed, and sharpies tried hard te seore. Immediately alter the home forwards took up the running, and transferred to the other end, where Bartley missed by inches. Barlow gave to Dawson, who banged It In, Robin just saving in time. Then Whitehouse had a pot. which Jones handed over. From the corner kick Dawson just shot outside. Earlestown kept up a hot attack on the Wirepullers' goal Bartley centred well, and the ball Was passed between Barlow. Diwloll and , Leach, with the result that Leaeh scored the first goal for Earlestown. After this the Warrington forwards visited the other goal, but the defence was sound. Earlestown again ran dawn and Bartley put In a beautiful centre, and from the resulting scrimmage in the good Dawson put the ball in the net for the second time. After this Warrington pall a fly- ing visit to the home goal, but Chew and his defenders were safe, and caused the Earlestown quintet to assume the aggressive again. The terrible eondition of the ground pre- vented tile teams from giving anything like a good exhibi- tion of the game, and the consequence was that play was rather tame. Leach ran down, but had hard lines. Barles- town then bombarded the Warrington goal, but Robin effected a number of marvellous saves, for which he was loudly applauded. The Visitors again eased the pressure, but Bartley came sway again and passed across to centre. where with an open goal 'settle Bent high over. Rariestown continued to have much the better of the argument. From a corner Whitehouse sliot straight for goal, lontalobin again kept his c ,arge Intact. The players then Indulged in a bit of mud-larking in fruit of the War- rington goal, but could not keep their feet, and several chances went abegglng. Warrington broke away, but Dawson, initiated a run down, but Leach shot wide. War- rington then visited Chew, but the ball weld behin I. Dawson raced away, but was badly fouled. Robin gave a grand display between the sticks for the Wire-pullers. War- rington broke away once more, arid Cllbborn knocked the ball with his hand. A penalty was given, and Sharpie& scored Half-time.—Earlestown two goals, Warrington one goal. In the second half play opened directly in favour of Barlestown and after several futile essays, a clever move- ment In which Dawson was the leading operator resulted In Rarlestown's third goal being notched. Warrington next had a turn of attacking and Sharpies forced Chew to fist away. The home custodian saved a low shot, and a speedy return to the Warrington goal saw Robin maintain his brilliant form saving innumerable shots in fine style. Barlestewn scored a fourth goal before the Core, and finally won by feur goals to one.

div.head: PREFERMENT FOR THE REV. E. R. TARBUCK.
div.p: PREFERMENT FOR THE REV. E. R. TARBUCK.
Acceptance of an Altrincham Living.
"A Great Wrench."

The Rev Ernest R Tarbuck, B A, vicar of St Paul's, Warrington, has been offered and has accepted the living of St George's, Altrinchsm, the patron of wh'ch is the Ven Arcudeacon Gore, vicar of Bowdon. Mr Tarbuck, who was appointed to S; Pan's, Warrington, in 1899, was formerly curate-in-charge of All Saints', Al:root:am, so that he is by no means a stranger to the district. Ha short period of ministerial work in Altrio- &tam was eminently successful and it was with great regret that the congregation of All Saints' received the announcement of his removal to Warrington. St Paul's Church has been vigorously worked under the present Vicar and his staff, the organizations being many and successful. There are excellent day schools, with ac- commodation for over 1,000 scholars, now earning the fullest possible grant ; evening continuation schools, with over 200 students ; large Sunday schools at both ends of toe parish, two communicants' guilds, several men's and youths' Bible classes, mothers' meeting, three peony banks, two Bands of Hope, a Girls' Friendly Society, with 246 mPmbers and over 100 associates, Parish Msgszines, crick.t and football clubs, Fcc. At present schemes are on font for a Parochial Hall and Church Institute ; for enlarging the accommodation at All Saints' Mission ; for a refreshment bir, to supply the men at tte works of Messrs Pearson and Knowles with meals and the best non-alcoholic drinks ; and also for the establishment of boys' trfen'a and women's social clubs, Church Lad's Brigade, it?. Mr Tarbuck's departure will be greatly regretted by his numerout Warrington friends. At Altrincham he will succeed the Rev W M B Lutener, who has resigned the

Preaching at St Paul's Church on Sunday evening the Rev E R Tarbuck made allusion to his impending de- parture. After a summary of the principal events which had occurred in the parish during the past twelve months, the rev gentleman said :—" And now, after such a recital of satisfactory progress, it is doubly hard for me to have to announce my early departure from amo agile you. It ii only nine days ago that! received the offer of a most important living. My mind has been in a turmoil ever since, but after being visited by the Vicar of the parish, and after consulting the patron, my own wardens, the Bishop, my late Vicar, Archdeacon WOOSI24M, and many others of my own personal iriends, I felt that it was a real call which I ought not to resist. But it will be a great wrench, and yet we must look at it in another way, I think. It is not only an honour to me to be asked by a patron whom personally I have seldom spoken to, and pressed to accept by a Vicar whose heart is set on gttting what he considers ne right man to follow him, but it is also an honour to the parish and especially to our .workers here. Had you not most loyally and enthu- siastically seconded my efforts in this parish I should never have been thought of, and it should be a source of comfort to you my dear friends to know this. You cannot do a better work for the church than to loyally second every good effort of your clergy that whenever they may be promoted to the more important parishes, you may consider it to be the very stamp of God's approval. Many opportunities will be afforded me, and an especially, favourable one, on the first night of our annual tea party of talking about our future plans, but I cannot close this long sermon without thanking you from the bottom of my heart for your three years' loyal friendship and unfailing support. I would end with the text as I began :—" Exhorting them to continue in the faith." Lets xiv. 22 I would ask your earnest prayers that the Holy Spirit may guide the trustees to appoint a better man than myself. Your prayers will, I know, follow me and support me in the discharge of my new duties. In the meantime I promise you that this parish shall cot ne left without clergy to carry on the work until the arrival of the new vicar.

The Queen-Regent of Spain has signed a decree. the chief provisions of which re.—No military officer under the age of twenty-five years may marry ; no officer under the rank a Captain may marry unless he can show that his private income added to his pay exceeds the pay of a captain.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.
WARRINGTON LOSE BY A POINT AT WIDNE3.

After their heavy ho Idly programme, Warrington were only able to place a week team in the field at Widnes on Saturday, Hallam. Isherwood. Allen and Burgess all being absentees. Widnes had Peacock off, Bown filing the vacancy. A large number of spectators accompanied the Warrington men' though the weather was vile. At Widnes the ground was found to be in a terribly wet and sloppy state, and a game of only 6) minutes veal played. The teams were as follows. Widnss : Kinsella. full back ; Hughes, Taylor, Tilley and Bown, threequarters ; Lally and Douglas. Lad backs, Atpey, Hampton, Moss, Riley, Curtis, ldignty, IrDonald and Lynch forwards.
Warrington : Knight, full-back ; Fish, Rateliffe, Dicken- son and Harris, three-quarters ; Townson and Hockenhall, half-backs ; Boardman, Morrison, Taylor, Rdmondson, Fell,

Eden. Knight, and Ashton. torwards. Swift started for Warrington against the wind,and Fish at once ran down to the Widnes line. From the ensuing scrim- mage Hockenhall charged Laity's kick down and scored near the corner. Fistaltook:the kick at goal and sent the ball under the cross-bar. Widnes at once rushed to the other end where Ratcliffe) was slow and the ball was charged down again. Knight only just sending dead in the nick of time. Dhkensora punted back again, but Widnes were soon on the aggressive once more. Knight was caught In possession near the line, and Warrington being penalised, the next minute Tilley placed a goal. This eneonragedithe home team who,side.d by the wind, gave the Warrington defence a lot of trouble Knight was more than once in difficulties but kept the line intact. Play was of a scrambling order, neither side show- ing much science Half time WarringtOn one try, Widnes one goal Warrington were expeeted to Win comfortably on changing,ends but they appeared to lack energy,wnile Widnes strained every nerve to get the lead. Warrington were forced bick and a scramble saw Hughes within an ace of scoring. Fish steppe 4 in however and dribb'ed to the cen- tre. Widnes were soon back again and got another penalty, Tilley doing the trick once snore to the joy of the home Crowd, which numbered but 3,00). Warrington now roused themselves and Fish went halt back. The ball was passed along to the left wing where Hookenhall missed a promising opening. Warrington attacked hotly and Fish was grassed on the line A weak kick saw Dickenson secure at the quarter line and drop at goal when a pass to Harris would probably have resulted in a try. Widnes cleared just as the whistle soun4e3 its final note, leaving them winners by 2 goals (4 points) to Warrington one try (3 points).

div.head: NORTHERN LEAGUE.
div.p: THE NORTHERN LEAGUE.
RUNCORN v. SALFORD.

This match was played at Runcorn in dirty weather before a poor crowd. Runcorn had to again take the field without the assistance of Houghton, The teams were representative and the grouad was in a shockinw condition. The visitors set the game going but the Runcorn f ont rank at once made tracks for the Salford line where a score was nearly effected by Walker. A brief incursion into the home terri- tory was neatly stopped by Moran. For some time Runcorn were iteot en the defence but the visiting backs though combining finely could find no opening. Furnival shone conspicuously in stopping several dangerous rusbes. At a critical moment Smith saved, Lomas breaking away andiWilkinson'replying.The home contingent still kept the " Reds' on the " qui vie" and the ball hat to be touched down. A Series of tall kicking left the advantage with the visitors. Play settlet down at midfield and some smart play was exhibited by both sides. Half time arrived with a blank sheet.—Langley started the second hal and a fine round of passing between the Runcorn backs almost enabled Butterworth to score. Warder was upset after steering his way throcgh is host of opponents. The Linnets wee not, however, to be denied. Jolley got possession and fine combination between Richardson. Butterworth, and Moran enabled the latter player to score a few minutes from the start. Moulton failed from a difficult angle. By smart following up Run- corn were forced on the defence. Give and take play fol- lowed. Varty marking. Lomas kicked a goal from an easy position. Play was evenly contested after this but judicious combination again resulted in Moran scoring at the corner. Moulton failing to augment. The Reds payed strongly and the leather visited each end In rapid succession. Exciting play fellow-d Runcorn eventually wining by two tries (6 points), to Salford 1 goal (2 points).

div.head: SWINTON V HUDDERSFIRLD.
div.p: SWINTON V HUDDERSFIRLD.

The return match between these clubs took place on the Swinton ground, before a fair number of spectators. Both sides were strongly represented, but the game lost much of its interest through the wretched weather and the sodde state of the ground. Hulderrfield won the toss. and Valen- tine kicked of for Swinton uphill and against the wind. Quickly the visitors forced their way close to the home line, where Dewhiret made a capital opening for Deere, but he threw the chance away through falling to take the pass. After Deere had missed placing a penalty goal the Swinton backs got going, and Cooper was brought down by Ready- hough when he appeared certain to score. Swinton then attacked strongly, but when the interval arrived, neither Hie hat scored. Early in the second half the visitors' three-quarters made a splendid passing movement, which almost ended in a score, Kitchen being tackled on the home line. Gradually Swinton worked their way back, and for the remainder of the game completely overplayed their opponents. DM Davies initiated several fine passing move- ments, from one of which Cooper scored a try. which Preston improved. The same player also followed up a gcod dribble by Ponta, and scored another try, which Preston again improved, and the game ended—Swinton. two goals and two tries (ten points) ; Huddersfield, nothing.
BROUGHTON RiNGERS V. HALIFAX.

This return match was played on the Rangers' ground, before only a moderate number of spectators. The home team played as selected, but the most noticeable absentee on tbe visitors side was Little, their full back, whilst at the last moment it was found that one of their forwards was unable to plarand they turned out with only fourteen men. A continuous do ortpour of rain caused the ground to be very soft and slippery. tand it was with the greatest difficulty the players kept on their feet. whilst accurate passing was almost Impossible. The Halifax backs scarcely passed the ball all through the game, but relied principally on their forwards, who, although a man short, played capitally tbroughout. The Rangers, on the other hand. were contin- ually passing and repassing the ball, with the result that very shortly alter the game bad commenced Wilson had crossed the Halifax line twice and had placed the ball behind the goal posts, W James, however, failed to add the goal points, although the place kicks were in the easiest possible positions. Winskill scored a try for Halifax, and at half- time the Rangers led by six points to three. In the second half the passing of the Rangers' backs completely baffled the visitors, and Wilson scored his third try, after he and Hogg had passed and repass-ed ths bill three-parts the length of the field WJames kicked a goal, and hen Kitaon seized an opening through a mull by Fielding, and scored a try for iltlffax. which Rigg failed to improve. Jackson added an- other try for the Rangers. the final soore being—Broughton Rangers, one goal and four tries (14 points) ; Halifax, two tries (sin points).
01.7..ELLA1 •V. HULL.

This match had been postponed on caturday on account of the Oldham ground being frozen, and it was played on Tuesday at Oldham. before about 10.000 spectators. Hull were fully represented, while the Oldham team was re- organised, Arthur Lees (half back) playing centre and Brady going behind the scrummage inhls place. Williams. after a lengthy absence, reappeared In the team, which in- cluded several reserve players. Oldham earted, and after a sharp dribble by the hull forwards into the home quarter the visiters were penalised and Ferguson kicked a goal. After this success Oldham played with renewed vigour. and their performance showed that the arrangement of the team was the most effective yet tried. After several attempts Oldham scored. Brady dodging over from the scrummage. Ferguson failed at the long and difficult kick. At the interval Oldham led by five points to nil. In thesecond half Oldham proved superior in scoring powers, although the Hull team played a good game. Lewis, Jscques. Driscoll, and Ham- brecht showed excellent combination In running and passing, but they failed to pierce the home defence, while Spottis- woode and Williams each scored a try, Ferguson aiding the two goals. The success of the Oldham team by 15 points to nil was very welcome to the supporters of the club, as the team has had a long run of failure during the last two months.

From a rush by the home isirwards Evans scored another try, which Preston again im- proved, and the game ended :—Swinton, two goals and two tries (ten points) ; Oldham, nothing.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
Manchester and the Irish Trade.
Live Stock to be Landed at Latchford.

The steamers running between Manchester and Dublin have maintained during the past year a steady and increased service. Never at any time since the steamers began to run has the traffl; gone back or remained at a standstill. Large shipments of Irish provisions are brought into Manchester regularly by thia route, parti- cularly butter, bacon, eggs, vegetables, and potatoes. Considerable quantified of oats, hay, and straw, malt, whisky, and stout are also handled, and from the interior of Ireland a large quantity of round timber is being carried. Without doubt this now popular route is doing a good deal, to promote increased business between the two countries ny affording advantageous rates for carriage. One very important teature of the traffic is the live stock shipments. Cattle, sheep and " pigs are brought in great numbers, not only for the Manchester market, but also for the interior towns of Lancashire, Yorkshire, and the Midlands, and for places as far distant as Norwich. Horses travelling by this route (and thus avoiding transhipment) always arrive at their destination in good condition. The live stock traffic has increased to such an extent that at times the steamship company has tad great difficulty in coping with it. The Company's pens at Dublin and Mode Wheel are commodious and well arranged, and animals that,bave to be entrained for interior English towns are transferred to railway trucks alongside the steamer. The necessity of driving them for any dis- tance or through the city, which is unavoidable by other routes, is thus obviated. Arrangements have also been made for livc stock from Ireland to be lanc'ect weekly at Latchford and Irlam, At Irlam a landing stage has been erected for the purpose, which enables consignees in thar district to have the stock discharged practically on the own farms. From the Manchester Docks large shipments of boilers, machinery, electric trams, and railway stock have been successfully trans- ported during the year ; some of the consignments were of very great sizl. 'roe regularity of the sailings and the substantial saving in carriage has gained for the Ship Canal route an important traffic in heavy drapery, S:c., from the Manchester home-trade houses to Dublin and all parts of Ireland.

div.head: PENKETIH CHILD'S DEATH. ---- Sad Case of Poverty.
div.p: A PENKETIH CHILD'S DEATH. ---- Sad Case of Poverty.

An inquest was held at the " Red Lion " Inn, Penketh, on Monday, relative to the death of John Holden the five weeks old child of of Mediae, Holden, 50, Bail House Cottages, Toe Ceroner said the jury bad rather a curious case to inquire into. The deceased was the illegitimate child of Mrs. Holden, who was a widow, and it appeared that on Monday, December 23rd, in consequence of eometoing which he heard, the police sergesni sent for Inspector Flackett of the N.S.P.C.C. and with him went to the: house of Mrs Holden. They found the child was dying and death took place on the following morning. Inquiries were made as to whether the child bad died in a nataral way or through neg'ect and Mrs Holden stated Una she first of all fed the child with the bottle I but as it could not assimilate milk, she tried condensed m I with the same result. As the child got weaker she sent for Dr Murray who told her that the baby required nourishment and advised her to go to the Woikhouse. Several people who lived in the neighbourhood said they had heard the woman saying things that were hostile to the child. I He (the Coroner) proposed to call the doctor to give , evidence, and unless he told them that the cause of , death resulted from negligence it would be no U 69 thrashing out the question of negligence. Margaret Lloyd spoke to attending Mrs Holden at her confinement, and said that when born , the child was healthy. Mr 3 Holden was in poor cir- cumstances. Witness attended her for a week and during that time the child was treated properly. Dr Murray gave the jur; the result of his post moptest examination. He said the child weighed 51lbs, which was not abnormal for a very weak child. There were no external marks eL,f bruising. Death was due to bronchitis, pneumonia, and pleurisy, if there was no other evidence witness was not prepared to say that death bad been brought about by neglect. The Coroner said that in face of what Dr Murray had said he could not see how a charge of manslaughter could possibly be sustained. He would leave the jury Ito decide whether they could arrive at & verdict without hearing any further evidence. , After discussing the matter for about twenty minutes , the jury request eel that further evidence might be given. ' Arlo Heath, wife of Peter Heath, provision dealer, Warringtoa-road, who resides near Mrs Holden stated that she was in toe back yard on Friday night,December 20th, when she heard deceased is:Teaming. She " heard the child lose its breath " and Mrs Bolden said "I'll learn you to wait. Fel see if I'm going to be ready for your mouth as soon as you optn it you glutton." Witness added that she weighed the child soon after its birth and it weighed Ellbs. In answer to the Carona' witness stated that she knew Mrs Holden's parish relief was stopped when she was most sn need of it, and she had no money except what she earned herself. Jesiie Stanley, another neighbour, said that Mrs. Holden had been very much despised owing to her mis- fortune. Witness considered that the woman did her duty to the chill as well as circumstances would allow her.
Aftrr further consideration the jury returned a verdict of Death from natural causes.

div.head: POLIsH SETTLEMENTS IN
div.p: POLIsH SETTLEMENTS IN
LANCASHIRE.
Some Interesting Small Communities.

-- --- Our great cities keep an open door for all comers who are willing to work and bear the burdees of the com- monweal. Nothing is more hopeful in society te-iay than the diminution of international prejudice. Scat- tered about Manchester are to be found people belonging to almost every civilisecl• nationalLy earth, and here and there among the small Lanca- shire towns and villages there are small colonies of foreign folk happily settled among us and living of quiet industry. In one or two of the colliery vil- lages in the neighbourhood of Newt m-le-Wiilows there are several small groups of Poles and L'teuan- lane, not numerous enough to form separate communi- ties, but quietly fellowicg the customs of our c.iuutry while nut forgetful of their own. The greater number are emigrants from Lithuanian Poland, or that part cf Poland almost exclusively inhabited by Lithuanians. These people have always been known for a submissive- ness of character. They are constantly seeking fresh fields, in America, in Germany, and in England, and they make the best of things wherever they go,wearing down the hereditary prejudices of the natives by quiet continuance Some 170 Lithuanians and Poles nave settled in the three villages of Elaydock, Ashton-in- Makerfield, and Peasley Cross, working as labourers in the pits thereabouts, and for the most part showing themselves worthy of the reFpf ct of their ceighbours. Most of these people come from the Suwalki district, in the North-east of Poland. which is almost entirely inhabited by Lithuanians. Up to the last partition of Poland Suwalki formed part of Lithuania, and it is cut off from the rest of Poland by great swamps. I: is not easy to explain the exact cause of their coming here, still less ot their choosing these Lancashire villages as , their tomes. Some of them came over so long ago as the great emigration of Poles and Lithuanians which took place after the failure of the Polish-Lithuanian rising in 1863. Many left tome for America ; others found a haven in London and Liverpool. Some of the Lithuanians now working in the collieries about St. Helens have found their way out from Liverpool, where they had worked in the sugar factories. Work becoming scarcer there, they carae to the colliery villages, where it was more abundant, and got employment as unskilled labourers. When they had settled down their relatives came from Poland and Newel them. The new-corners in recent years have been mainly young mcn who .have fled to escape forced service in the Rusiian army. Greeter 'than the unhappiness of living among strangers is the antipathy to the Russian conquerors. A return to Polani means arrest as a des .rter, so many of the exiles give up all hope of going home again. They settle down, and perhaps marry English wives. The Litlauaniars who seek their fooe. tunes hero have in their own country been for toe most part agricultural labourers. They were practically in the condition of serfs, fed and clothed by their mascers and paid a few pounds a year in wages. They enjoy the freedom and independence they find in E iglaud„ and as they are bumble-minded and easily contented few of them regret the change. They are almost with- out exception devout Catholics. The only ornaments you see in their houses are images or pictures belonging to their faitb.

A group of Lithuanian families is to b 3 found in a new street in Havdock within a stone's throw of one cf the collieries. They live very much to themselves. They know little English, and that isolates them from their neighbours. They are for all that a cheery and open-minded people, and they are always ready to take the visitor into their houses and treat them with a simple courtesy. Those who know them best describe these Lithuanians as warm-hearted peasants with strong religious feeling, and symnathetic and generous to others in distress. They are not well educated ; their Russian masters make no provision for learning. Their language is proscribed in Russia, and any books ia Lithuanian have to be smuggled over the German frontiers. For all that, most of them have learnt to read, and a few of them can wrfte. They are very ready to talk about themselves. Visiting the Haydock colony the other day, I came across an especi- ally engaging young Lithuanian of the characteristic tye—florid and blue-eyed. Thrusting a shining morning face through the door, he besought a little English girl to act as interpreter, and so gave me his views. He was a farm labourer in Poland, but " living very poor " there. You may work from Christmas to Christ- mas and earn only three or four pounds. Displaying his neat suit of brown, be said "These would he Sunday clothes in Poland." " Nice country, England," said the young Lithuanian. and his compatriots standity, round smiled assent. In another house was a gaunt Russian peasant, sitting peacefully among the hereditary foes of his race. His view of life was resigned, and his phr- risolohY monosyllabic. There was also a lively boyish Lithuanian who inquired anxiously, " What fn• you come ?" He smiled incredulously when told,and aqcet with earnest repetition, " What for you come ?" I had much friendly Ghat with a burly young fellow who spoke bitterly of the Russian rule. The Russian sat stolidly and made no sign of opposit'on. In Ashtan-in-Makerfield, a few miles away, there are several small colonies scattered about. The number of Lithuanians is about the same, but here aro one or two families of Poles. These Poles come more usually from the towns. They do not understand the Lithuanian language, are generally better educated.and of a quicki and enthusiastic though somewhat fickle temperament. While the Lithuanians are unskilled labourers, the Poles are often trac:esmen—especially shoemakers, tailors, or joiners. The proportion of Poles to Lithuanians is everywhere small. In Haydock, Ash- ton, and S. Helens it is 18 ;id Liverpool, where there are 600, 17 ; while in Manchester, of 400 of tle-se people, the percentage is 14. The immigration is said to be now almost stationary in this district, although fresh families arrive now and then. For instance, a group of Lithuanians turned out of the train at Ashton the other day, possessing not a word of English, and with no direction except the name of the street where their friends live. They were guiled thither by the friendly police. Immigration is increasing to Sc,,tland, where the favourite place of refuge is Glasgow.—." Man- chester Guardian."

WARRINGTON G.P.O. ST AI-F SOCIAL

A most successful reunion was held at the Winmnr- leigh Cafe on Thursday last week,at which Learly 100 of the staff and their immediate friends were present. At ball-past five a "high" tea was provided after which a long and successful programme was got through. Dancing was vigorously kept up until the early hours of the morning. . . . . . . .

The Postmaster who tork the chair at tea, said in the first place ; I thank you most heartily and sincerely for asking ma to be amongst you this evening. I am /glad to see a larvr number of the staff present this year. I hope that the alteration in the arrangements will fully meet the varying wants of all. Your invitation is keenly appreciated because I feel it bears a special sig- nification. I regard it as the expression of your loyalty as a proof of your confidence and as cony eying an earnest dfsire that the harmonious relations that have hitherto existed may continue la the future. It is a real pleasure to be able to compliment the staff upon the efficient manner in which the work has been di,- posed of, despite new and increasing difficulties. 'leis year we have had obstacles in respect to weather to contend with, then we have to deal with a considerable addition of parcels and letters whilst the congested space at our disposal remains the same, but I have rt lied and not in vain upon your hearty cc-operation your unwavering determination and above, perhaps all your enthusiasm to resclutely coos with and to successfully overcome these yearly increasing and special difficulties A few remarks as to the new office. Some time since I as many of you know made urgent representation as to the immediate want of more accommodation. Those representations were favourably received and negotia- tions were fet on foot to obtain a suitable site. I hope the acquisition by the department of such a site will , soon become vn fait acco»zpli and that at bo distant , date we *all have an office suited to the growing r - quirements of the town, providing for future develop- and in which more favourable conditions exist fur
_ ment a.. ~,, '-' • I dischargi

Asci,“ ging the various duties. The necessity for a new office after the lapse of con-,paratively a short period marks an important fact, in which we all rejoice, v z , the great increase in the population and the commercial prosperity of the town. Numerous have been the changes amongst us during the present year, we have lost the chief clerk, assistant superintendent and other senior officers. For Mr Broadhurst the late chief clerk I shall always entertain feelings of the greatest respect. In my opinion no man was governed by higher ideals of honour, justice, by alty, and impartiality than he. He valued the esteem cf his fellow men and especially of those amongst whom he laboured but he placed a higher worth upon the approval of his own conscience and upon the clear and complete consciousaess the tir7l conviction that he had striven faithfully to fulfil his duty. I wish him well in his new sphere of labour and lam convinced that in his future work he will reflect credit upon the office in which he commenced his career and in which for so long a period he has laboured: But there is no reason to fear that any deterioration will result from these changes. The efficiency ot the office 5e5t5 upon a wider haqs upon broader and deeper foundations. It depends, in my belief, more upon the recognition and acceptance of the alit:anon on the part of each member of the staff, that not only should Le for personal reasons strive to perform his duties satisfac- torily and see that his conduct is exemplary, but that be should do this out of respect to the staff of which he is a member. and for the regard of the office to which he belor gs ; and•further that the constraining .Jfect of this obligation should lead him to take an interest in the progress and welfare of other members of the staff. If this spirit be inculcated and fostered, if one be actuated by this high sentiment and animated by this lofty ideal of duty, there need be no apprehension that tbe ton. i the Warrington Office will be lowered, or that its effic ency will be impaired. As to the recent app intments it was very gratifying to me that the recommendations I had made, backed by the powerful support of our respected surveyor (Mr Salisbury) had met with the approval of the Postmaster General. I wish each of the officers success, and trust that in the no distant future further promotion will await them. And now permit me to wish you all a very Happy New Year, and may the remembrance of this social add a further ray of gladness, and may much permanent good remit from it. Hearty votes of thanks, to the Committee were pro- pr.sed in suitable terms by Mr J4ues (chief clerk), and were graeefully responded to ,by Miss Richaids and others.

div.head: EAR LESTOWN & NEWTON'
div.p: EAR LESTOWN & NEWTON'

THE CHILD MESSENGER'S BILL. In connection with this Act which came into force on Wednesday the let instant the Publicans of Earlestown and Newton have decided not to, serve any child 'under the age of 14 years, with ) intoxicating liquors, under any circumstances whatever. POLICE CASES. At the Newton Police buildings on Monday before Mr T J Gillespie, Adam Hart of Haydock, Edward Mannion of Earlestown and Edward Roberts of Newton were charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Earlestown on Saturday night, and were each fined 23 61 and costs. A BOY'S NARROW ESCAPE. On Tuesday morning when the van belonging to the Earlestown Co-operative Society was going its usual round of delivery in charge of Frank Dougherty, a lad named Joseph Mason who was accompanying the van tripped whilst the horse was in motion and fell, the wheel going over the thumh of one of his hands, breaking it. He had a very narrow shave the wheel just missing his head. ROWDY SPECTATORS AT A FOOTBALL MATCH. On New Year's day morning, during the progress of a football nie,ch between Burtonwood and Lon- don and North-Western wagon shop, at Earlestown, the spectators crowded on to the touch line and impeded play. The linesman, B Glover, remon- strated with them, but without effect. He then spoke to the referee who stopped the game until the line was cleared. Several roughs in the crowd resented this with the result that they attacked Glover with sods, mud, stones, &C., an drove him from the groand. He had to seek police protection, and had to have one eye attended to, owing to an injury. NEW YEAR'S EVE AT EARLESTWN. A more miserable night could not well be imagined than that which witnessed the departure of. the old year. Rain began to fall soon after six o'clock, and it never ceased until some time during Wednesday morning. Con- sequently the streets were deserted, except for a few roysterers who haunted any place of shelter they could find, and annoyed otherwise respectable people with songs and shouts not appropriate to the occasion. Watch-night services were held at all the places of worship, but they were not very well attended, the inclemency of the weather probably being responsible for this. W INWICE EDUCATIONAL FOUNDATION. The result of the examination held on December 7th.for five exhibitions offered by the governors of the above foundation has now been announced. I' C Singleton, of St Peter's Schools, Newton, and Joseph B Atkinson, Wesleyan day schools, Earles- town, have each gained a Winvvick Exhibition of £l5 per year. George Howard, Church school, Lowton St Mary's, Percy Barnes, Parish Church schools, Lowton, and Harold Gerrard, Independent Methodist .school, LOWtOO, have each gained a Lowton Exhibition of the yearly value of £l2. Each of the exhibitions are tenable for two years at any schools other than Public Elementary Schools approved by the governors.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT
EARLESTOWN.
[BY A COEILESPONDENTI,

Notices have been issued broadcast by the Publicans of this district having reference to the Child Messengers' Liquor Bill,aiad if the people are not made fully aware of its provisions and penalties it is not througk any fault or remissness ont he part of the publicans. The latter have met in solemn conclave and have decided not to serve any child under the age of 14 years, with any kind of intoxi- cating liquors, under any circumstances whatever. This appears to be the mode of procedure all over the country, and it is evident the publicans do not intend taking any risks.

For the size of the place Newton has contributed its fair share of victims to the South African war. A good number volunteered in the Imperial Yeomanry, and amongst the fint lot which went out, several were killed. Of the second lot who departed early this year, news has come to hand that young Will Frost of the 32nd Company, 1,Y., has succumbed to enteric fever, He was a promis- ing young fellow, and his loss is a sad blow to his parents. Since the receipt of the intelligence of his death a letter has been received from him in which the poor fellow gives a bright view of his life, and cheerily refers to his home coming.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Warrington were the visitors to the Mesnes ground on Saturday, and although the Wirepullers played a plucky and determined game, they had to acknowledge themselves beaten by a superior eleven. Of course it was fully expected that Earlestown would win comfortably and this they did, although for the major part of the first half, the visitors had quite as much of the game as their opponents. The field was a veritable quagmire and correct football was out of the question. Under the circumstances the pace from the beginning to the end was unusually fast. Both goals were under water whilst mud lay thick all over the ground. Play had been in progress ten minutes when a long shot from Whitehouse stuck in front of Hobin in the mud, and Dawson dashing up, appeared to have the goal at his mercy, but he slipped before be could get control of the leather. Barlow next got possession but he repeated Dawson's performance and it was left to Leach to net the ball. Ten minutes later Dawson received a pretty pass frena Settle and turning rapidly round, banged the leather into the corner of the net with terrific force llobin not hav- ing the slightest chance of stopping the flying leather. Just before the interval Sharpies made a bee-line for the bonze goal, and passed the leather to Riley, Clibborn knocking it down with his hand. The ensuing penalty was easily placed past Chew by Sharpies.

Resuming, Earlestown quickty got the upper hand, and goals were scored by Barlow and Daw- son, and Warrington retired defeated by four goals to one. The one outstanding feature in the play of the W ire-pullers ;was the exhibition of Hobin in goal. He gays one of the finest displays between the sticks ever seen on the Mesnes ground. Shots innumerable were rained in upon him, especially during the last few minutes of the first half, but each of them he dealt with in masterly style. But for his fine custodianship, the visitors would have suffered a much heavier defeat.

St Helens Town Club visited Earlestown on New Year's day, this beirg the first meeting of the teams in a League fixture. On two other occasions in Cup ties this season St Helens have beaten Earlestown, but each .time the match has been played at St Helens. Consequently the meeting on Wednesday was looked forward to with especial interest, a good game being foreshadowed. Nearly 2,000 people turned up,and the Earlestown finances received much needed help. The game from start to finish was very fast, each side striving their utmost to gain a lead. Earlestown, however, played a magnificent game and asserted their superi- ority early on Settle notching the first point. For only a very short period did St Helens do any pressing and this after they had scored a goal through a mistakeby Cottam, but when Dawson with a low swift shot put on a third goal for Earlestown, there was never any doubt as to the issue, and the game ended in favour of Earlestown by 3 goals to 1.
The Rovers visited Sutton Commercial, and were defeated by three goals to nil.

Haydock received a visit from Southport Central on Saturday, but the home dressing room which is situated under the stand, was flooded with water. Naturally the visitors declined to dress in such a Place, and as no other suitable place could be obtained which would be handy to the ground, the referee decided to abandon the match.

Theft of an Offertory Box—Warrington Man Sent to Penal Servitude. At the Lancaster Quarter Sessions on Tuesdays James Towey, 36, of Warrington, for stealing an offertory box and three penny pieces at St. Peter's Catholic Church, Lancaster, was committed to five years' penal servitude. Prisoner was caught in the corfessional trying to get the coin out of the box -with a piece of wire, but bebore he could succeed was arrested by the organist. The priest's box was emptied a day or two before. He had 28 previous convictions at Liverpool, Warrington, and Run- Corn.

div.head: CHILDREN'S FANCY
div.p: CHILDREN'S FANCY
DRESS BALL.
Brilliant Scene in Parr Hall

New Year's Eve was damp and dePresaing, but within the walls of Parr Hall everything was bright and cheerful. Never before has such a brilliant scene been witnessed in Parr Hall, as that which attended the Children's Fancy Dress Ball, given by the Mayor and Mayoress (Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Parr.) In deciding to delight the hearts of the juvapile portion of the community, and to bring them into touch with the civic life of the town, Mr. Parr has followed the example set by Mr. Alderman James Fairclough on the occasion of the Jubilee of her late Majesty, Queen Victoria, when a similar func- tion was held but not on such a lavish scale as that which marked Tuesday evening's proceedings. Thoge who beheld the living wealth of colour as it mingled and co-mingled in the phantasmagoria which was presented will not readily forget it. The dresses worn were superb in construction and design. The characters represented ranged " from grave to gay, from lively to severe " in tact all that ingenuity could devise and deft fingers provide was to be seen in great profusion. Bedecked, ornate and gay, the merry children " filled the air around with beauty" and one almost wished that he could be young again. The youthful guests, numbering nearly COO, were received by the Mayor and Mayoress on the plat- form. The duty of annmncing the names and the characters represented devolved upon the Chief Constable, who discharged his duties with dignity aud precision. At the outset the Mayoress was presented with a basket of choice flowers,tastef ally arranged, the gift of Alderman Bolton. The pre- sentation was made on behalf of the children by Miss Mabel Tunstall, a wee mite charmingly attired to represent a Rose Queen. She was escorted on the platform by, Master Graham Wilson, (a son of Mr Stanley Wilson, the deputy Town Clerk) who ap- peared as Admiral Lord Collingwood. The Mayor wore his chain of office and had a pleasant look or word for each child, whilst the Mayoress won all hearts by the kindly and gracious manner wit:e which she discharged her onerous duties. Having paid their respects to the Mayor and Mayoress, the children passed down the steps in the centre of the platform into the body of the ball. Here they were arranged by a number of stewards and stewardesses for a grand serpentine -march, which commenced immediately after the reception was over The reception occupied over an hour and the large number of onlookers showed their appreciation of any effective make-up by warm-hearted applause. When the last name had been called and the chil- dren were grouped together in the body of the hall the ensemble was pleasing in the extreme and the effect was considerably heightened when the children began to march in serpentine fashion with Miss Eleanor Parr dressed as a Norwegian peasant and Miss Lister Kaye as a water nymph at the head. This was followed by a grand march past the Mayor and Mayoress, and the van-coloured spectacle, representative of characters of a bygone age and of to-day, excelled in beauty and effective- ness anything seen on the pantomimic stage. The next item was a polka to the strains of the sprightly music of " The tin gee-gee." The music was supplied by a small orchestral band conducted by Mr Percy Randall. The ensuing dances included valses, galops, lancers and Highland schottisches. When tired of " tripping the light fantastic toe " the youthful masqueraders were free to adjourn to the refreshment buffet where such toothsome edibles as turkey and tongue sandwiches, lobster and shrimp patties. and numerous delicacies were served with tee, coffee or other drinks suitable for children. This department was in charge of Mr and Mrs Powis. The hall been vary tastefully decorated by Mr Ralph Johnson, and Mr Parker, the head gardener of the Corporation, had introduced a number of choice plants from the Park. Excellent arrangements had been made for the safety of the children. Where fires were provided in the ante- rooms, fireguards were put down and a staff of clerks from the Town Hall rendered assistance in the cloak rooms. The ball continued until eleven o'clock when the children,tired but happy,departed for home. At the close of the function Mrs Parr wished all her youthful guests "A happy and Prosperous New Year." Thus ended what mast be to all who participated in it, a memorable event which must ever be a pleasing recollection to them. The general public were allowed to view the pro- ceedings from the galleries and the platform. The platform had been set apart for the use of the mem- bers of the Corporation and their wives and fami- lies, magistrates, and friends who were attired in evening dress. The demand for tickets by parents of the children and their friends was in excess of the accommodation of the galleries. The Town Clerk and Deputy Town Clerk endeavoured to meet the wishes of all by issuing transfer tickets. This enabled spectators on leaving the hall between the hours of 7 and 11 to hand their tickets to their friends,and consequently more people than the hall would accommodate at one time were enabled to witness the charming spectacle. The following gentlemen gave their services as stewards : Mr Roger C Parr (Master of Ceremonies) Captain Appleton, the Town Clerk, the Chief Con- stable, Mr El Owen, Mr L Fairdough, Mr R Fair- clouph and Mr G Roberts. In addition, the follow- ing ladies rendered valuable assistance: Mrs J,, Lyon Whittle, Mrs Stanley Wilson, Mrs Talbot,'Mrs F R Pierpoint, Miss Parr, Miss Willis, Miss Fair- dough (Barryfield), Miss Mabel Fairclough, miss Dora Fairclough (Latchford Grange) Miss Roberts, Miss Milling, Miss Owen and Miss Lyon Whittle. Played at Wigan on Thursday. Leigh were without Pear- son and Dunbayin. Wigan won by 8 points to nil.
ASSOCIATION.
WARRINGTON DISTRICT LEAGUE,
LATCHFORD' V BEWSEY ALL SAINTS.

Played at Latchford on Saturdsy. In the first half the locals had much the best of it, and opened the scoring from a penalty kick, this being the only point scored. In the concluding stage Price added a second, and Latchford won by two goals to nil. WARRINGTON TRINITY' V FRODSHAM.

—.— Played on the ground of the former on Saturday. The start was delayed owing to the visitors arriving late. Hough- ton set the ball rolling for the home team, who at once got down, Bradshaw shootinz outside when in a favourable posi- tion. The visitors then bore down on the home goal, and a corner occurred, but this was got safely away, and a fine bout of passing between Houghton, Lavell and Baker, saw the last named give the Frodsham custodian a difficult shot to negotiate. The visitors attacked strongly, and had it not been for the fine defence of Joseph and Shearer a score would have been effected. Half-time Warrington Trinity, nil ; Frodshans, nil. On the resumption, the home team were the first to show up, Lavell with a good shot opening the score five minutes after the interval. Warrington were having by far the better of the game and Lavell scored a second point as a result of a movement initiated by Baird. After some smart work on the part of Dickenson. Bradshaw added another point, the visitors custodian having no chance whatever to save. Baird was now responsitsle with a good run along the touch, and after eluding several opponents sent In a good shot, from which the ball was beaded through, Baker sent in a screw shot, the ball eventually finding the net. Just before time Lavell made a tricky run, and beating all opposition scored the sixth and last point. Warrington Trinity thus won a one-sided game by six goals to nil.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF
GUARDIANS.

This Board met at the Workhouse, Warrington, on Wednesday morning. Mr A J Jolley presided and there were also present :—Mrs Clay, Rev Father Wilson, Dr Murray, Messrs G Pilling, William Hickman, T H Ash- croft, William Mather, S Davies, William Houghton, A Brookes, J Clarke, A Jolley, T Halton, R Forshaw, Backhouse, with J C Sutton (clerk), 8 Sutton (assistant clerk), A Wright (superintendent Padgate Schools), C H Ward (Workhouse Master),

div.head: COMPLIMENTS OF THE SEASON.
div.p: COMPLIMENTS OF THE SEASON.

The CHAIRMAN said before the business was proceeded with he would like to wish everyone present " A very happy and prosperous Now Year." Mr HICKMAN thought the members oughll to recipro- cate the- compliment by wishing the Chairman and Vice-chairman" A very bright and happy New Year." (Hear, hear.) HOUSE COMMITTEE.:

div.head: KEEPING OF THE WORKHOUSE BOOKS.
div.p: THE KEEPING OF THE WORKHOUSE BOOKS.

At a meeting of the House Committee, the Clerk was instructed to advertise for Master and Matron. Tee appointment of Miss Florence Wagstaff as a probationer nurse at a salary of £l2 per annum with uniform. rations, &c was made. It was ordered that workhouse inmates have tea and bread and butter for breakfast and supper on Christmas Day. It was furthur recom- mended that the water in use at the workhouse for boiler purposes be analysed; that the Clerk apply to the Local Government Board for approval of payment to the Workhouse Master of 103 per week, in lieu of official diet, by reason of his serious illness ; that Mr P Jocelyn of Bletchingley, Surrey, be temporarily em- ployed to keen the Workhouse books upon the follow- ing terms :—lf living at the House, &c., 21s per week, if outdoor 30s per week, appointment determinable by one week's notice, travelling expenses each way to be allowed. The committee also recommended that the sum of £6 6s be paid to Mr J Barron for services rendered in connection with workhouse accounts during the Master's illness. Mr BROOKES moved the confirmation of the minutes Mr PILLING seconded. Mr ASHCROFT moved an amendment rescinding the resolution referring to the allowance of 103 per week to the Master in lieu of rations. He stated that the Board was already paying wages to somebody else every week for work which ought to be done by the Master. He did not think any private employer would treat his workpeople as generously as they svcr3 treat- jog Mr Ward. Mr J CLARKE seconded the amendment. In answer to a question by Mr Eficxmarr, the Crum- MAN pointed out that each resident officer was allowed I rations and the rations were estimated to be worth 104 a week. Mr Ward was unable to consume the rations I provided according to the dietiry scale of the Work- house. It was therefore suggested that Mr Ward might be allowed the money value of the rations. The matter was discussed by the House Committee and the majority of the committee was in favour of making the allowance. Mr HICKMAN said he was satisfied with the answer' given. He would like to ask whether the allewance would make any difference in regard to superannuation? The CHAIRMAN No. Mr PILLING pointed out that the only food Mr Watd had been able to take out of the rations allowed him was milk. He had had to buy expensive and specially prepared food. Mr HICKMAN spoke in favour of the proposition, and after further discussion the amendment was lost and the minutes of the committee confirmed.

A DEPUTATION. It was decided that t:ie chairman (Mr A J Jolley), the chairman of the House Committee (Mr A Brookes) and the senior vice-chairman (Dr Patterson) represent the Board at the conference of representatives of Lancashire Boards of Guardians to be held at Manchester on Tues- day neat for considering the important question of lunatic accommodation. This was all the business.

Fatal Falls Downstairs at Warrington. Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, conducted an inquest in the Board room at the Workhouse on Monday,touching the death of Harriet McKeen (52) 11, Albert-street, who died in the Workhouse in- firmary as the result of a fall downstaira on Novem- ber 2nd.—The evidence was •to the effect that at 10.30 p.m. on the date named deceased was going to bed when she fell from the top of the stairs to the bottom. She was medically:attended hut in order that she might receive better care and attention she was removed to the Workhouse Infirmary where she died on December 28th. Dr Braids made a tost morlem examination and found that death was due to a fracture of the skull causing inflammation ,of the brain. A verdict of "Accidental death " I was returned.—The jury then inquired into the circumstances attending the death of Michael Grady (9), 69, Birchall-street, who died in the infirmary on the previous Saturday. Thomas Grady, the deceased's father, stated that his son was a tanner's labourer. On Monday night, December 23rd, deceased came home under the influence of drink and went to bed leaving witness in the kitchen. About 11 o'clock he got up and was going down stairs when he fell to the bottom. He did not appear to be much injured and went back to bed. On the 27t12 December he complained of pains in the head and was ultimately removed to the Infirmary where he died.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

div.head: NOTES ON LIAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON LIAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist."

Leigh are in the South-West Lancashire Competition! So many people have been in doubt about this, includ- ing myself, that I must set everybody right, on the authority of the Northern Union official handbook. Warrington have therefore lost two matches in this competition, those played on the Leigh and Widnes grounds. They still possess the best record, however, for they have only Widnes home, and Wigan home and I away to play, and by winning these matches they 'should still secure the medals. Widnes, who have not yet lost in this competition,have to play Runcorn away, Warrington away, Leigh home and away, and Wigan away. Judging by their form on Saturday,l cannot see them getting many points out of these matches.

Widnes were in high glee at, maintaining their un- beaten certificate on Saturday, when they got the better of Warrington by a single point after a close struggle in the mud. Worse weather could hardly have been specially prepared for the occasion, rain falling heavily nearly all the morning, and during the greater part of the afternoon. The ground was, therefore, best described as " tripey," and the 30 minutes play each way was about as much as either the teams or specta- tors desired. There was a good gate—one of the best at Widnes this season—and quite a quarter of the number were Warrington enthusiasts, whose desire to see Warrington play on every possible occasion has been intensified by recent successes.

Warrington were unfortunate in having to take the field minus four regular backs in Isherwood, Burgess, Hallam and Allen. The difference between their ability and that of the substitutes would easily have won the match. It was at half-back mostly where Warrington were let down, Townson and Hockenhall making only poor use of the ball when they got it, while the for- wards played as if they had had quite enough football for the week. When Warrington scored in the first five minutes they seemed to think they had the match in hand and took matters very easily. Widnes were far the keener side and eventually came out on top, though only by the aid of two penalty goals. When necessary I think Warrington can give their neighbours a severe drubbing.

By the way Fish is not playing up to form, and I rather fancy he is not trying very hard. Certainly his indifferent attitude on the field has been freely com- mented upon of late, and Jack's popularity will rapidly wane unless he bucks up. Dickenson is also showing a tendency to selfishness, Rarris being the most con- sistent player at present. At Widnes he was neglected and might easily have won the game had Dickenson parted once instead of dropping for goal. On the Widnes side there does not seem to be a great deal of class,Tilley and Kinsella being the smartest exponents. The former is an ex-Association player and has de- veloped into a very fair Rugby centre with unusual skill as a place-kicker. Kinsella is a good full back, and quite outshone Knight who is too slow at fielding for first-class football.
The South-West Lancashire League table up-to-date is as follows :
Point P. W. L. D. For Agst. Pts. Warrington 7 ... 5 ... 2 ... 0 57 37 ... 10 Widnes Runcorn 5 2 3 0 17 27 4 Wigan Leigh St. Helens 6 1 5 0 29 51 2

Warrington fell from the pinnacle of fame with a most resounding crash on New Year's day, all through a littte affair with Bradford at Wilderspool. Having beaten the big Bradfordians at Park Avenue earlier in in the season. Warrington anticipated no difficulty in repeating • the performance, but they had to reckon with quite a different side this time. The Bradford fifteen was practically the same, but their form had altered to a startling extent. From the first they set about whacking Warrington in a style which boded ill for the home lot. Pollard scored in the first quarter of an hour, and though Fish soon equalised the Brad- fordians lost no time in getting ahead again. At half time they led by eight points to three points, and in the succeeding stages of the game they made hacks of the home defence. Tries were run in and goals kicked or missed with alarming frequency, and the final score only just fell one short of 20 points.Warring- ton managed to aggregate eight points and that was all.

It was really a remarkable game and I do not remem- ber such another at Warrington, except the memorable encounter with Kingston lovers—the latter then a second division club—when they won by 20 odd points with ridiculous ease. The Bradford men are a some- what similar lot, being exceptionally big and active, and on Wednesday they seemed to. have had a dose of H G Wells' famous'' accelerator," so full of enthusi- asm and dash were they. Nothing went wrong with the Bradfordians. scarcely, once they got into their stride. Even when Heseltine went off hurt it was only an extra misfortune for Warrington, because Broadley, the visiting skipper, came out of the pack and played Hades behind the "scrum," The beautiful bouncing Broadley and the ball seemed to be part and parcel for one another, and the Way he romped over the Warrington line on three occasions as startling for a 15 stone man. One of the three tries was dis- allowed, but it was a try all the same and the most deserving of the lot, for Broadley won a 50 yards race with .he Warrington backs. Bradford probably played some way above their normal form, but there is no dis- puting the fact that they are a fine side now they have shaken down properly, and on the day's play they out- classed Warrington.

The Warrington men only seemed able to get going by spasmodic bursts,so that the fact that 8 points were scored is not discreditable. Fish bagged the lot, his two tries being real beauties, but the hero of the game, in my opinion, was•once more Burgess. The Flixton youth played magnificently and made an opening for Fish that would have done credit to an international. He has come on immensely of late, and without him on Wednesday Warrington would have been in a sorry plight. Hockenhall is not at home at half-back, and the absence of Hallam, Townson, Morrison and Fell, was severely felt, especially as Isherwood was hardly fit to have turned out.

It is rather curious that, after having kept their lines intact through five matches, Warrington should have the goal line crossed five times in one match. The boasted defence looked a very flabby thing on New Year s Day,

Spectacularly the game was a treat, fast open foot- ball being played by both sides. Seeing that Hunslet won at Salford, and Huddersfield at Leigh, it is evident the Tykes have learnt something and mean to make a big effort to wipe off some of the heavy debt run up against them during the first half of the season. Hull went down with another bang at Runcorn, but they still hold second place. Warrington have dropped from third to sixth, and this place is the one they are most like to fill at the end of the League tourney.

The Professional Sub-committee has been busy again,with the result that Swinton and Runcorn look very much like being penalised, while Hunslet are under suspicion. As Swinton have already lost two points, this additional offence will not please their supporters.

The cases of Swinton and Runcorn are already settled, so far as the Professional Sub-committee is concerned. Swinton and B Murphy, one of their players, have been found guilty of a breach of Sub-section C of Rule 1, which say s Every professional shall be in bona-fide employment, and shall not be allowed to play Rugby football unless following such employment in a bona-fide manner. If a man is away from work through exceptional circum- stances, he must not play until he has received a special permission from the Professional Sub-committee.

Runcorn's offence comes under Rule s,which is to the effect that" no professional shall be allowed to play for more than one club, whether affiliated to this Union or not, in any season, without the permission of the club to which the player belongs." Messenger is the player implicated, and he has been suspended.

The breaches of law on the part of these clubs neces- sarily means the deduction of points, provided, of course, the General Committee confirm the findings,for By-law 28 of the Northern League says— Any club found guilty of a breach of the Professional Laws shall have two points deducted from its score.

ISEQUEL TO A BENEFIT CONCERT. At Shaw some time ago a benefit concert was organ- ised by the operatives at the Beal Spinning Company's mill on behalf of James Marsden, a joiner-minder, who had long been ill, and about whom most of those who knew him entertained the gloomiest fears. An Oldham press representative who saw Mr Marsden at his home, 76, Fraser-street, foundlhim a lusty, alert man, whose appearance certainly gave no indication of the troubles through which lie had passed. A couple of years ago he fell ill (he said), and was attended by a most skilful doctor, who diagnosed his complaint as consumption of the bowels. The medicine he received gave him no relief, and eventually, as he was getting weaker and weaker, a second medical physician was called in consultation with the first. Still there was no improvement, and Mr. Marsden was now reduced to such a low condition that everyone gave him up. "I could never get my wind," said Mr Marsden,"and in walking across the kitchen I had to lean heavily on the shoulders of one of my children." In October he was induced to give Dr Williams' Pink Pills a trial. After four days Mr Marsden began to feel lin some degree better, and then, as be got stronger, he was able to take short walks. He took eight or nine boxes of Dr. Williams' Pink/Pills, and by this thee he felt as well as ever he did.

Oa Dyson's Dioramas and Gipsy Choir. There was again a large audience at Parr Hall on Saturday evening to witness the capital entertain- ment provided by Mr Joshua Dyson and his Gipsy Choir. The pictorial subject was "The Boer War," and it was dealt with in a highly interesting manner. The singing ot the choir was excellent, several of the items being of a patriotic and military description. On Sunday after- noon and evening sacred concerts were giten, the programmes embracing anthems, illustra- ted songs, violin qolos, duets, sleigh bells, and auto-harp selections. On Monday even- ing the dioramic subject was " Australia " and a first rate programme was submitted, The conclud- ing entertainment was given in the Co-operative Hall on Tuesday evening when there was a large audience. Mr Dyson lectured on "America "and the members of the choir acquitted themselves in their usual creditable manner.
